text:
Good morning. I declare open this hearing of the Community Affairs Legislation Committee's inquiry into the 2026-2027 supplementary budget estimates. I begin by acknowledging the traditional custodians of the land on which we meet today, the Ngunnawal and Ngambri people, and pay my respects to their elders, past and present. I extend that respect to any Aboriginal and Torres Strait Islander people here today.

The committee has fixed Thursday 17 December 2026 as the date for the return of answers to questions taken on notice. The committee would appreciate if senators could provide any written questions on notice to the secretariat by Thursday 5 November 2026. The committee's proceedings today will begin with the Department of Health, Disability and Ageing on whole-of-portfolio and corporate matters. The committee will be conducting today's hearing in person and via teleconference. Under standing order 26, the committee must take all evidence in public session. This includes answers to questions on notice. I remind all witnesses that, in giving evidence to the committee, they are protected by parliamentary privilege. It is unlawful for anyone to threaten or disadvantage a witness on account of evidence given to a committee.

agency: Department of Health, Disability and Ageing

text: I'm interested about what happened to the health resourcing division. It appears as if it's gone into the Systems Strategy section with the exception of Medicare Benefits and Digital Health. Is that correct?

agency: Department of Health, Disability and Ageing
text: We had the Health Resourcing Group. It's a group, not a division. That was previously. The deputy secretary who had been in charge of that for a long time was Penny Shakespeare. There were five divisions within that group. There was TAD, the technical assessment division. There was the Medicare benefits and digital division. There was the immunisation and the emergency response division. That's not quite the right title, but that's essentially what it is. There was Workforce Division, and there was Benefits Integrity. Benefits Integrity went across to Health Products Regulation Group, which is the group that—the largest part is the Therapeutic Goods Administration, but it also has some compliance functions. The Benefits Integrity Division, which is essentially compliance systems functions, looking after things like MDS, PBS, pharmacy et cetera, went to there. The TAD, I'm better at the acronym than the thing, the technical assessment division, which does things like service PBAC and MSAC et cetera, went into the Systems Strategy Group, as did Workforce, and the Medicare and digital and that immunisation and emergency response went into the group that is—I think it's been renamed. It was primary care. Someone could prompt me what it's actually called now, but it's the group that already has things like the urgent care clinics.

witness_position: Secretary

agency: Department of Health, Disability and Ageing
text: Good morning, department and Minister. While we're on corporate matters, does the department have a specific policy on the use of AI? If so, can you summarise that for the committee, please?

agency: Department of Health, Disability and Ageing
text: Yes, Senator. We obviously are bound by the whole-of-government policies in that regard, so we reference those. We also have developed our own processes and policies around assurance of AI, for example, and its use. We are continuing to educate staff on that. Inherently, the approach is about ensuring that it is used responsibly, and that includes ensuring that staff remain accountable for all outputs and the responsible use of AI.
witness_organisation: Department of Health, Disability and Ageing
witness_position: Chief Operating Officer

agency: Department of Health, Disability and Ageing
text: In terms of whether it's policy or it's the corporate side of things, are you using it for everything across the department, or are there limitations on where you won't use it?

agency: Department of Health, Disability and Ageing
text: Staff have access to a licensed version of Copilot. About two-thirds of our staff have taken up that opportunity. They are routinely using AI Copilot in that context to help them with day-to-day tasks. For uses beyond that, we have a structured approach to a register of use cases that have to go through a risk assessment and impact assessment process. If it's going to require investment, we also need to look at the cost benefit of that, in terms of whether it is an efficient use of resources to actually make that change. We are progressively looking at that. We're not looking to rush into investments or uses without properly assessing the impacts that they might have and ensuring that they are beneficial and meet those sort of expectations around responsible use.
witness_organisation: Department of Health, Disability and Ageing
witness_position: Chief Operating Officer

agency: Department of Health, Disability and Ageing
text: Recently, we've seen issues about patches having to be applied to government websites and the like. What safeguards have you got in place for AI for commercially sensitive information like private health insurance numbers? You've got a number of med tech companies with the prosthesis list, those kinds that are interacting with government. What are the safeguards that you have to ensure that commercially sensitive data or personally sensitive data is also not being accessed or misused by bots or the like?

agency: Department of Health, Disability and Ageing
text: We have a long history, obviously, of responding to any suggestion that there may be weaknesses in our systems or in our protection of that sort of data. AI changes the game a little bit in terms of the pace at which those weaknesses can be identified and taken advantage of. It doesn't create new weaknesses; it just means it's a lot faster to actually utilise them. We are very closely engaged and responsive to any advice from the Australian Signals Directorate and ensure that we're rolling that out. For example, with the recent issues last week with PHP and with web applications, we did patches within 24 hours of that advice and additional patching over the weekend to improve the security of some of our web applications in response to advice from the vendor and ASD, as well as to improve our monitoring across those to make sure that we're able to detect any issues. We have a specific program of work we are initiating now that is looking particularly through the lens of frontier AI at the exploitation of weaknesses that it may be able to accelerate in regard to our systems.
witness_organisation: Department of Health, Disability and Ageing
witness_position: Chief Operating Officer

agency: Department of Health, Disability and Ageing
text: In terms of any Department of Health websites, what patches? Was there anything identified that was of significant seriousness that it needed patching? You mentioned web applications. Was there anything else?

agency: Department of Health, Disability and Ageing
text: It happens progressively. The most recent one with PHP—it's a language that's used primarily for web applications, and there was a global vulnerability identified. We applied the patches there and increased the monitoring across any applications we have that utilise that language, which is consistent with what's happening across government. We did that quite quickly. We're very conscious of the need to balance the need for quick action with the risks associated with making very abrupt changes to IT systems. You can sometimes cause more harm than you're trying to address. We also are conscious that there may be times when we need to take systems down to protect the information within them while we work out a patching scenario. That's certainly something we consider.
witness_organisation: Department of Health, Disability and Ageing
witness_position: Chief Operating Officer

agency: Department of Health, Disability and Ageing
text: Just rounding that out, in terms of the recent OpenAI breach of Medicare data, what conversations have you had with DSS around any gaps or issues there?

We don't use AI generated images and those sorts of things. We make sure we're using images of real Australians, so we routinely commission people to refresh those images for us, so that they are of actual situations—in this case, in aged care.

witness_position: Chief Operating Officer

agency: Department of Health, Disability and Ageing
text: Yes. Can we have the number that were produced. Also, as my colleague requested, how do people receive that? Is it mailed to them? Does the RAS or the assessor provide that? How does that work? How does that actually get received?

agency: Department of Health, Disability and Ageing
text: There will be a range of different ways. We do public-facing communication activities. For example, we have pop-ups in shopping centres, libraries and things like that to actually consult with older people. The magnets are often handed out as part of that consultation, reminding people—giving them guidance about My Aged Care, but also something to be able to make contact later.
witness_organisation: Department of Health, Disability and Ageing
witness_position: Chief Operating Officer

agency: Department of Health, Disability and Ageing
text: I have some questions around this year's budget, which includes funding for public hospitals and disability. Can you outline what this agreement means for the funding of public hospitals across Australia?

agency: Department of Health, Disability and Ageing
text: I'll ask Ms Street to come to the table, but, broadly speaking, if I give the high-level answer, it provided an additional $25 billion above the baseline to states and territories over the next five years, allowing growth and expenditure from the Commonwealth to rise up to eight per cent per year, providing resources for the public hospital system to meet the needs of citizens.
witness_organisation: Department of Health, Disability and Ageing
witness_position: Secretary

agency: Department of Health, Disability and Ageing
text: You said $25 billion?

agency: Department of Health, Disability and Ageing
text: Yes.
witness_organisation: Department of Health, Disability and Ageing
witness_position: Secretary

agency: Department of Health, Disability and Ageing
text: And over how long?

agency: Department of Health, Disability and Ageing
text: Maybe I'll hand over to Ms Street. That's the additional amount. The actual total funding is well over $200 billion.
witness_organisation: Department of Health, Disability and Ageing
witness_position: Secretary

agency: Department of Health, Disability and Ageing
text: Okay. Thank you.

agency: Department of Health, Disability and Ageing
text: It's $220 billion over the five years, starting from this financial year. It's the funding under the National Health Reform Agreement.
witness_organisation: Department of Health, Disability and Ageing
witness_position: Deputy Secretary, Systems Strategy Group

agency: Department of Health, Disability and Ageing
text: My question was really about that extra funding, the $25 billion. What does that mean for the funding of public hospitals across Australia?

agency: Department of Health, Disability and Ageing
text: I'll pass over to Mr Hawkins in terms of the breakdown, but, in terms of the additional funding, it is additional funding into the hospital system and into all the other reforms that are under the National Health Reform Agreement. We can provide the indicative split by state and territory. It is activity based funding, so it will be—
witness_organisation: Department of Health, Disability and Ageing
witness_position: Deputy Secretary, Systems Strategy Group

agency: Department of Health, Disability and Ageing
text: I would like that, if you could provide that information.

agency: Department of Health, Disability and Ageing
text: As Ms Street said, there are two frames to the numbers. There's the additional funding that's provided, which is the $24.4 billion. Then you've got that as an addition to what was historically provided, so the totality of that is the $220 billion. In terms of the $24.4 billion, we can give you an indicative breakdown of what that looks like per state and territory. New South Wales was an additional $6.5 billion; Victoria, $5.8 billion; Queensland, $5.7 billion; Western Australia, $2.4 billion; South Australia, $2 billion; Tasmania, $625 million; ACT, $557 million; and NT, $741 million. That's the total additional $24.4 billion and where that went across the jurisdictions.
witness_organisation: Department of Health, Disability and Ageing
witness_position: First Assistant Secretary, Portfolio Strategy Division

agency: Department of Health, Disability and Ageing
text: Thank you for that information. I'm having a look at the media release. How does the agreement help secure the future of the NDIS?

agency: Department of Health, Disability and Ageing
text: The key part of the agreement is that all first ministers agreed that they would be targeting a five to six per cent growth rate of the scheme in terms of annual funding growth of the NDIS. The NDIS in recent years had been growing by up to 20 per cent per year. It is now a program of around $50 billion a year, so that was a very significant component. There was also an agreement to progress further work on foundational supports and to embed the agreement on the Thriving Kids program. Those are programs outside the NDIS which also provide services and take pressure off the NDIS, which was a key recommendation of the Paul and Bonyhady review in 2023 as a way of ensuring that the NDIS was not the only way in which disability support was provided in Australia.
witness_organisation: Department of Health, Disability and Ageing
witness_position: Secretary

agency: Department of Health, Disability and Ageing
text: Sorry, I should have said I was asking more generally about the National Health Reform Agreement. In addition to the extra $25 billion above the baseline of $220 billion, in what other ways is the government looking at taking pressure off hospitals? What other programs have we got in place?

agency: Department of Health, Disability and Ageing

agency: Department of Health, Disability and Ageing
text: Senator, there's clearly a funding component to the NHRA, but there are also significant reforms within that agreement that were signed up to. For example, there are reforms within the agreement relating clearly to improving First Nations outcomes, and what we call schedule B, which is around the arrangements for us to work with the coalition on a range of measures to support First Nations communities. There are mechanisms within that. There's an agreement to setting up and looking at innovations in health care. It's what we call the service model reform funding stream. So there's work going on with the states and territories looking at what innovative care looks like and how that could be utilised more broadly across—
witness_organisation: Department of Health, Disability and Ageing
witness_position: First Assistant Secretary, Portfolio Strategy Division

As you can imagine, with this type of money, with a range of different streams, there is a very complex program of work that we've signed up to collectively do with the jurisdictions, and we're working through those in a measured and coordinated way, working closely with our state and territory colleagues.

agency: Department of Health, Disability and Ageing

So, whilst we talk about the NHRA being around funding and hospital funding, actually it goes to a broader way in which the Commonwealth will work with the states and territories on health system outcomes.

agency: Department of Health, Disability and Ageing
text: My questions relate to the IAT, and the first lot are in relation to some of the documents that had been previously released under FOI in relation to that. My first question is this. According to emails that were published under FOI, the department was regularly indicating to assessors that human override would be preserved. I'm keen to understand more clearly how this miscommunication happened. I know that we've heard in our inquiry hearing that there was a point up until which people were being advised that override would be there, and then it wasn't. I'm keen to understand now if the department has actually unpacked how that miscommunication came about.

agency: Department of Health, Disability and Ageing
text: The government made its decision in 2024 that there would not be a human override and established the mechanism by which the integrated assessment tool and rules would be used to do classification and prioritisation. That was the key decision that government made at that time. What happened after that was a departure from the legal grounds on which the system was created and then the way that the build was done in terms of IT. Then there was a further departure, which we acknowledge and apologise for—it was unfortunate—in providing the guidance to assessors that there would be a human override. As you would appreciate—and it's been the subject of many appearances—this was a very big set of reforms. At the end of that process, when doing the readiness and doing the assurance checks, we became aware that this departure existed, particularly in the provision of legal advice that happened at the end of September, right before the new system was due to start on 1 November. Subsequent to that, there were a number of options that were considered around this misalignment between the government decision, the way the system had been built, what assessors had been advised and options were considered and what legal advice had been provided. What happened was that we had to give notification to those assessors that an error had been made and the guidelines had to be changed and that there would not be a human override. So that is the way that that occurred.

text: Thanks, Ms Stewart. That accords with the evidence that was given at our Senate inquiry. agency: Department of Health, Disability and Ageing

agency: Department of Health, Disability and Ageing
text:
I'll probably just supplement Ms Stewart's response. As Ms Stewart has identified, the development of the legal framework did involve a number of parallel processes. There were a number of different teams. We were working at the same time to develop the legislative framework, IT system, program arrangements and operational policies. As Ms Stewart has said, the department has acknowledged that there was not a consistent understanding across teams about whether or not there would be an ability for the assessor to override the home support algorithm outcomes. We have accepted in response to the Ombudsman's report that a common understanding of the legal framework across all teams is essential. We accept responsibility for not meeting that standard.

That said, when it comes to the IT build, we've given evidence in this forum and in other inquiries over the last several months around the fact that the system needs a functionality to enable outcomes to be overridden to put people into short-term pathways, such as restorative, end-of-life and also residential care. The way that we've managed the ability for someone to not override an ongoing Support at Home classification 1 to 8 is to have a very clear and prominent warning sign that says, 'If you override this outcome in relation to this subset of classifications, that is illegal.' We are basically monitoring that approach. That is the way that has come into development and the way that we're managing the system in practice.

witness_position: First Assistant Secretary, Home Care Division

agency: Department of Health, Disability and Ageing
text: Can I just add to this to be helpful?
witness_organisation: Department of Health, Disability and Ageing
witness_position: Secretary

agency: Department of Health, Disability and Ageing
text:
Just to clarify, I'm still unclear, though, that the department has identified and can tell the Senate who was responsible for the error. You've told us there was a miscommunication. You've told us the build had human override built into it. But no one has actually said that you've identified where the problem precisely existed. I'm going to go to page 12 of the Ombudsman's report, where the Ombudsman says:

• In our view, the Department did not, and may still not, understand key components of the legal framework it created, nor

did it understand what legal framework it was meant to create. This had serious consequences, including that up until the

introduction of the Act and the Rules in October 2025, the Department had been incorrectly advising assessment

providers and the public that automated IAT outcomes could be changed. This is despite the fact that there was no

mechanism in the Act or the Rules to change outcomes.

My concern is, if the department can't tell the Senate precisely how this error occurred and who was responsible and the Ombudsman is saying they're not convinced that the department understood what it was meant to be doing, how can we be sure that these errors aren't going to happen again?

agency: Department of Health, Disability and Ageing
text: Thank you for the question. We have done quite a lot of looking back as to where we think the divergence occurred. We believe the divergence occurred as far back as June 2024 in terms of different understandings of whether there would be an override. So we have looked at planning sessions that went into the IT build where there was clearly an understanding by some in the department that there would be an override function. We agree with the Ombudsman that there was not uniform understanding of the legal basis through that period leading up to 1 November 2025. We wouldn't agree with the characterisation that the department doesn't understand the legal basis of the arrangements now. I think my colleagues have provided significant evidence to various committees of the Senate related to this that, once the checks were done before the launching of the system on 1 November 2025, there was clarity both about the legal basis but also across the whole department as to the fact that there would not be an override for that component of the IAT. So we have agreed with the recommendation from the Ombudsman to do a root-cause analysis, in which we will further investigate the precise reason for the divergence. But, as best as we can tell at the moment, the divergence occurred for some teams as far back as June 2024. Then unfortunately it became established wisdom among some teams that there would be an override. It was only when the final checks were done with the law just before commencement that this inconsistency was identified, at which point we then advised assessors that the override was not available.

agency: Department of Health, Disability and Ageing

No, sorry, Senator. What we've put into evidence is that there was a clear policy decision of government, which I said was in April 2024. At that point they were building a system to allow that. agency: Department of Health, Disability and Ageing
text: Senator, let's start with the problem that the government is trying to deal with. It has a number of dimensions. The first is that the demand for aged care, including aged care that people can receive in their own homes, is expanding enormously. The previous system for assessing people was really inconsistent, and saw different assessor organisations provide really unexplainable differences in both the priority and classification that they allocated to the people they were assessing. So the royal commission recommended that there be a single integrated assessment system, and that it included a tool. The tool that has been developed and is in use involves human engagement at every point; there are inputs that are made by trained assessors and they're across a large number of questions. It's a tool that's designed to provide fairer outcomes and it's delivering a very high volume. But we do accept that in any implementation arrangement, you always need to listen to the feedback that you're receiving from the community. We are hearing feedback from community on their concerns about this, and you'll know that Minister Rae has recently announced an implementation review of the assessment system. That's because older Australians and their loved ones have told us that the assessment system isn't always getting it right.

agency: Department of Health, Disability and Ageing
text: On 1 October, there was a significant change in terms of the government funding for the category of services for personal care, which includes things such as showering, incontinence and some of the wound dressing. I'll hand over to my colleagues to go into more details about that.
witness_organisation: National Health and Medical Research Council
witness_position: Deputy Secretary, Ageing and Aged Care Group

agency: Department of Health, Disability and Ageing
text:
In respect of personal care implementation, following the implementation of aged-care reforms in November last year—this is one of those examples where Australian government, the department, continue to engage with the sector to understand the impacts of the reforms and where there are opportunities to improve the aged-care system for older people. One of the things that we heard was that, for some people, the contribution required for personal care was not affordable, and so that was therefore potentially impacting on their ability to access it and therefore maintain dignity and choice. So government committed $1 billion over four years from 2026-27 to remove that contribution. And, as of 1 October 2026, people are now no longer required to pay. Effectively, that was progressed because it's got several significant benefits for older people—firstly, removing financial concerns as a potential barrier. So people who may have considered reducing, delaying or declining personal care on that basis—it was resolved. It's about improving dignity of care and quality of life. It is as Ms Stewart said; it covers things like showering, dressing, continence management, personal hygiene and assistance with medication.

Ultimately, the benefit here is about—it's reducing the risk with poor hygiene, skin conditions, infections, falls and functional decline, so it results in better health and wellbeing outcomes for people. It's about the Australian government's intent of the policy of the Support at Home program, which is to keep people living in their homes for longer and prevent that deterioration that could lead to people providing, if they're required to, higher levels of care. One of the benefits in this particular initiative is that it strengthened consumer confidence in the ability of the government to listen and respond to the concerns as we roll out implementation of the reforms. I'm not sure if my colleague Ms Barnett has anything further to add.
witness_organisation: National Health and Medical Research Council
witness_position: Acting First Assistant Secretary, Reform Implementation

agency: Department of Health, Disability and Ageing
text: Good morning, Senator. In terms of the numbers, we'd have to take on notice the specific number, but there's a very large portion of the Support at Home participants that are on grandparenting arrangements, so they haven't had to make contributions towards this. But then, as more people enter the system and people who were approved after that period in September 2024—it's that cohort that's going to benefit from this change primarily, and it will increase over time. So those people that have been making a contribution since 1 November won't have to from this point forward.

The Older Persons Advocacy Network and COTA, who deal with our very important participants every day, have really supported this change—and the providers as well. It's quite an intensely personal service, so people's being able to access that service at the time that they want to and their not having to make choices about whether they can afford the contributions or not will make a big change to a lot of people. The response has been very positive.
witness_organisation: National Health and Medical Research Council
witness_position: Acting Assistant Secretary, Reform Implementation

agency: Department of Health, Disability and Ageing

witness_position: Acting First Assistant Secretary, Reform Implementation

agency: Department of Health, Disability and Ageing
text:
Especially for women, who are predominantly the carers of their older parents or the people around them at home, I imagine it's quite a sharing of the load—for lots of women across Australia, too, with the people that they love in their lives.

You talked about how it's being received across the sector. Does this decision respond to some of the direct feedback that we've got from the sector, and what have the sector said in response to—I'm not looking for particular quotes, but it'd be good if you can share some of the positive feedback that you've got from the sector about why this matters.

agency: Department of Health, Disability and Ageing
text: Overall, the feedback has been positive. Like I mentioned, helping people as they're refreshing their care plans to look at going forward—what's the best mix of care for them in the home. Helping them pick services that meet their needs when they need them—all of the feedback has been positive around this change. It also, I guess, frees people up to maybe access other services within their package that they might not have been accessing because they've been making certain choices. Overall, it has been a positive change. Then, of course, as my colleagues mentioned earlier, we are continuously taking feedback on the service list overall for Support at Home, so there are opportunities open at the moment for people to provide feedback on other services as we continue to refine the program.
witness_organisation: National Health and Medical Research Council
witness_position: Acting Assistant Secretary, Reform Implementation

agency: Department of Health, Disability and Ageing
text: I can't remember if you've already talked about this. I wonder if you can talk about how important it is for older Australians to be able to get—you talked about their getting the support that they need when they need it. I wonder if you could talk a bit more about why it's important to give them the support they need to help them stay at home longer and what you've heard from older Australians about why that's important for them.

agency: Department of Health, Disability and Ageing
text: It's the underpinning principle of Support at Home—to get people to be able to exercise that choice to stay at home if they want to. Moving into residential care or accessing other types of care is a deeply personal choice, and there are multiple reasons why people would prefer to stay connected to their community, in their home, rather than move to residential care at a certain point before moving to those different care options later, if they choose to. So it's about choice, and it's about giving people the right supports to be able to stay home safely and comfortably.
witness_organisation: National Health and Medical Research Council
witness_position: Acting Assistant Secretary, Reform Implementation

agency: Department of Health, Disability and Ageing
text:
Further to what Ms Barnett said, one of the really key aspects of the reforms that were introduced on 1 November is legislation that puts the rights of older people at the heart of the system. That's really important in terms of trauma informed culture and giving choice and, if it is the person's choice and they're able to—and the wellbeing and the health outcomes in terms of ageing in place with community and kin. It is really important. I think that's a really fundamental driver for the work that we do when we turn up to work. Putting older people at the heart is such a fundamental premise.

One other aspect in terms of the feedback and what this means—one of the things that we work very hard to do is ensure trust and confidence in this system. I think that, by government listening to the feedback about the importance of that aspect of the service system and the contributions—taking on board that feedback and acting instils confidence that feedback is important and that it will be actioned upon in a timely manner. That continuous improvement that we're striving to do—noting that it is still not one year old, this system.
witness_organisation: National Health and Medical Research Council
witness_position: Deputy Secretary, Ageing and Aged Care Group

agency: Department of Health, Disability and Ageing
text: You are getting lots of good feedback. You used the words 'culture' and 'kin'. Particularly for First Nations people, that's really important. But, certainly, for lots of Australians, it's important to be able to receive the care in a place where you grew up. Often, especially if you're somebody who has created and built a life in regional parts of the country, moving to an aged-care facility might mean moving away from the community that you know and love and the family that you have created or been a part of for a long time. I suppose I'm interested in your comments about culture and kin. How does this keep people connected to culture and their families, particularly for First Nations people or people in regional and rural communities?

agency: Department of Health, Disability and Ageing
text:
There are a number of different ways that the new system seeks to do that. At the very heart of it is having—and government has legislated now for an ongoing First Nations commissioner. I think that's really important, and I acknowledge the work that Andrea Kelly did as the interim First Nations commissioner—and, now, Jodi Cassar. I start with that because that's so important around legislating an independent, statutory Indigenous person that thinks day in, day out about the care that First Nations people are doing.

It's not only about building the First Nations sector but about ensuring the cultural capability, because a lot of, as you know, mob attend services that are delivered by non-Aboriginal providers. And then there are a whole range of policies and programs throughout the aged-care system to ensure that Aboriginal people get the care that they need, once again, around choice. But I do acknowledge that, sometimes, in some of the markets, it's not completely possible. But we are really striving to do that—as well as around workforce initiatives. There's a trial on at the moment around assessment—having Indigenous assessment organisations for Aboriginal and Torres Strait Islander people—which is such a key entry point.

The final thing I would say is—and I acknowledge your very good last name; we might be related along the way. It recognises that, very sadly, our people age differently, and the entry into the system is much younger for our people. I think that's a really fundamental design element of our aged-care system in this country.
witness_organisation: National Health and Medical Research Council
witness_position: Deputy Secretary, Ageing and Aged Care Group

agency: Department of Health, Disability and Ageing
text: Absolutely. I think there are absolutely some unique not-so-good and great things about what it means to be a First Nations person who ages in this country. Then I think there are some things that are universal to all of us—wanting to age and grow older in the places that we know and love, being connected to culture and community and home—as well. I'm getting the 'wrap up' from the chair before I move on to my next set of questions, but thank you very much. I appreciate it.

agency: Department of Health, Disability and Ageing
text: We will go to a break. We will come back at 11.30 and continue with this same outcome.

agency: Department of Health, Disability and Ageing
text: Welcome back. We will recommence with outcome 3. Senator Allman-Payne.

agency: Department of Health, Disability and Ageing
text: Coming back to the integrated assessment tool, we've heard through our aged-care inquiries and statements made by the minister that the idea of the integrated assessment tool was to bring consistency to decision-making. Yet, in their report, the Ombudsman says that there's a contradiction in the sense that assessor expertise and judgement informs the inputs to the IAT, but then they're not allowed to consider the appropriateness at the other end. We've also heard from the Ombudsman's report that the department has what I think we could say is a distinct lack of oversight for assessor performance, which is actually critical to this whole process. So why have no human override at the back end of the IAT when the Ombudsman has said that it's not objective at the other end and the department is lacking in oversight of those judgements?

agency: Department of Health, Disability and Ageing
text: The secretary addressed this in his letter to the Ombudsman. The reason there's silence on our end is that we're looking for the reference in the letter. Excuse us for one—
witness_organisation: National Health and Medical Research Council
witness_position: Deputy Secretary, Ageing and Aged Care Group

agency: Department of Health, Disability and Ageing
text:
Perhaps I'll paraphrase what I said in the response to the Ombudsman. We acknowledge that assessors have a significant input on the input side, so they answer a minimum of 125 questions and up to 340 questions. One of the things that we wouldn't agree with the characterisation of the Ombudsman on is that he describes the department having a view that we think this is a logical and binary process. That's not our view. We do agree that there is a degree of subjectivity in the application of assessment judgement when they are considering the inputs to the IAT. That is inevitable to some degree.

What the IAT is trying to do is provide a structure to the assessment of people to ensure a greater level of consistency. But I think we would all acknowledge that there will be some variation between the assessors and the way in which older people with similar needs may present or provide information to assessors on the way through. So we are relying on that expert judgement. We're also relying on the fact that, when the assessment delegate is deciding whether to agree with the assessment, they will take into account, based on their judgement, information that is not just in the questions that feed into the algorithm but in the free-form text, which will inform their view about whether the inputs to the algorithm are giving the right outcome for that individual. That is something that has been difficult to communicate at times—the role of the free-form text—but it is critical in terms of providing additional information to the assessment delegate which would inform their view of whether the inputs are right.

Can I make one other point. The other thing is that, now that the government has allowed an escalation pathway, we are relying on those assessment delegates to form a view about whether this would be appropriate to escalate through that pathway because they would form a view that they think the holistic assessment does not accurately reflect the needs of that individual. Of course, they would also be taking into account the free-form text when they're making that assessment. So we certainly think assessors professional and clinical judgement is very important. As a department and in the way the policy has been enacted, we are cautious about a system that has unfettered discretion that doesn't have some boundaries around it because our experience under home-care packages is that this leads to very significant deviations from the criteria set for home-care packages. In the order of 25 to 50 per cent of times, the assessment was overridden, with significant variation between assessment organisations.
witness_organisation: Department of Health, Disability and Ageing
witness_position: Secretary

agency: Department of Health, Disability and Ageing
text: I want to be clear. The free-form text plays no role in the algorithm, though, does it?

agency: Department of Health, Disability and Ageing
text: No. Again, the free-form text doesn't enter into the calculation of the algorithm. But the free-form text is available to the assessor to then check in their own mind whether the inputs that are going to the algorithm are accurately reflecting the needs of the participant. That was the system prior to the introduction of the escalation pathway. After the escalation pathway was brought into effect—it's also the free-form text that would be part of the things that would inform the assessor as to whether they would trigger the escalation pathway.
witness_organisation: Department of Health, Disability and Ageing
witness_position: Secretary

agency: Department of Health, Disability and Ageing
text: I'm trying to understand why the government and the department have made a recommendation not to have human oversight at the end of the process other than through the escalation pathway. Wouldn't it be better, for example, to address the concerns that the Ombudsman has raised around actual checking of compliance with learning requirements and provider performance in relation to assessments? Has this problem been created because the government has privatised assessments, rather than having health assessors who used to do assessments doing them? Is this actually a function of going to a single assessment system that you've now created this other problem and, therefore, the way that you're fixing it is to put in a computer algorithm because there's actually not the proper quality assurance of assessments that should be taking place?

agency: Department of Health, Disability and Ageing
text: Perhaps I'll ask the team to comment. I think this issue of assessment oversight is a separate issue raised by the Ombudsman. We've accepted the recommendations to do more on oversight there. It's also the case that, even with home-care packages, there was a mixture of private providers and public providers, so the structure of that market is very similar. We agree with the observations of the Ombudsman. We need to do more. As we said in our reply, when we are in a new system—we were lighter touch on compliance, and then we intend to be going forward as we allow the system to come up to speed. But we will certainly be looking at increasing compliance and will work on learning outcomes on the way through. Maybe Mr Pugh or Ms Stewart would like to comment further.
witness_organisation: Department of Health, Disability and Ageing
witness_position: Secretary

agency: Department of Health, Disability and Ageing
text:
To that comment around privatisation and further on what the secretary said, there is a mixture of providers that deliver this very essential service in terms of assessment and entry into the aged-care system. Fifty per cent of those assessments are undertaken by our colleagues in the state and territory health systems. So they do 100 per cent of all of the assessments of older people in a hospital setting and 40 per cent in community settings, and the residual of that 60 per cent is made up from not-for-profit and profit providers. We completely accept the recommendation, as Secretary Comley has said, around the assessment organisation and performance.

One of the really important aspects of this is what we're moving from and to. Before the single assessment and these contracts were enacted in the new system, there were key performance indicators. There were only two, as I understand it, and they were largely self-assessed—so not independent or any other assurance. We're moving into, as we should, more robust key performance indicators that do have not only a level of them assessing themselves but also a high level of assurance and management on that.

Moving into this system, there are around 3,000 workers who are working on those assessments on any day around Australia around getting them trained, getting the guidance and getting the system up and running. There was a different approach to those KPIs at the beginning, and that is not the approach that there is now or the approach that there will be into the future. For assessment organisations that are not meeting those KPIs—I do note, though, that some KPIs do not relate to every assessment organisation depending on where they're doing that assessment—there are remediation plans that are in place that they will need to address properly.
witness_organisation: National Health and Medical Research Council
witness_position: Deputy Secretary, Ageing and Aged Care Group

agency: Department of Health, Disability and Ageing
text: The only thing to supplement the secretary and Ms Stewart is that we do have quite a strict governance framework in place. We will be monitoring the performance of assessment organisations and the operation of the Single Assessment System more broadly, including the independent assessment tool and the underpinning classification allocation and priority algorithms through our aged-care portfolio delivery board, and then also linking with the broader departmental governance structures. So I think the imputation that we don't have good governance is a little off.
witness_organisation: National Health and Medical Research Council
witness_position: First Assistant Secretary, Home Care Division

agency: Department of Health, Disability and Ageing
text: It's not my imputation; it's what the Ombudsman said. I'm just repeating back to you what's in the Ombudsman's report.

agency: Department of Health, Disability and Ageing
text: We will make sure that this is very much within the close remit of those various assurance and governance frameworks.
witness_organisation: National Health and Medical Research Council
witness_position: First Assistant Secretary, Home Care Division

agency: Department of Health, Disability and Ageing
text: Does the department have confidence that the integrated assessment tool is accurately assessing older people, particularly those with cognitive issues and mental health conditions?

agency: Department of Health, Disability and Ageing
text: I have a high level of confidence around the integrated assessment tool. I note that in the work—and we were talking about that before, Senator Allman-Payne, in terms of the rapid review that we were tasked with on the priority algorithm. There was feedback from stakeholders that were consulted as part of that around the integrated assessment tool. Government has acknowledged and tasked work around a review of the algorithms—the priority and the classification algorithms that work with the integrated assessment tool. But, in terms of its robust testing and its application, I have a level of confidence in that. It is not to say that we don't continually think about the integrated assessment tool or think about continuous improvement, but I've got a high degree of confidence with the integrated assessment tool.
witness_organisation: National Health and Medical Research Council
witness_position: Deputy Secretary, Ageing and Aged Care Group

agency: Department of Health, Disability and Ageing
text:
You mentioned robust testing. Page 12 of the Ombudsman's report says:

The Department implemented the IAT in its current form without any meaningful risk assessment, evaluation or analysis, despite the obvious risks that would arise with deterministic automated decision-making …

What do you say to that finding?

agency: Department of Health, Disability and Ageing
text: I think that the secretary might have addressed that in his letter, but I'm mindful that he's sitting next to me.
witness_organisation: National Health and Medical Research Council
witness_position: Deputy Secretary, Ageing and Aged Care Group

agency: Department of Health, Disability and Ageing
text:
I will refer to my reply to the Ombudsman because I think we have spent a bit of time thinking about how best to express this. I wrote in my letter to the Ombudsman:

In your draft report, you state that the trials and consultation on the IAT completed over several years did not support the development of the IAT in its current form and that "the Department implemented the IAT in its current form without any meaningful risk assessment, evaluation or analysis". The department does not accept this characterisation. The questions used in the IAT today were settled in mid-2023. They were then validated through 22,000 live trials in 2023, with minor modifications such as to the sequence of questions made post the live trials. The data from these live trials was used in the development of the classification algorithm. The IAT was also used to complete more than 200,000 assessments during 2024-25. The data from these assessments was used to refine and validate the classification algorithm. The IAT and supporting classification and prioritisation algorithms, as introduced on 1 November 2025, were therefore subject to significant testing and validation. This iterative approach to development is consistent with standard arrangements for major system changes. The alternate view would be that, following testing, the IAT should have been locked in its final form and then subject to extensive further testing. We do not believe that would have been practical and would have extended the implementation timeframe, delaying the benefits of the new system. We also note that we do not view the algorithms as final products. The Government is committed to ongoing review and monitoring of the system and intends to make any necessary refinements over time.

To your point about risk assurance, also, the government had significant governance assurance and risk management processes in place during the development of the Aged Care Act 2024 and associated reforms. My letter then said:

A dedicated Aged Care Transformation Steering Committee with cross-Government oversight and an independent assurer was established to monitor the implementation of reforms, including the introduction of the IAT. The reforms were also subject to independent processes, including the Senate Standing Committee for the Scrutiny of Bills. An Implementation Readiness Assessment was undertaken in September 2023, with two Gateway Reviews that followed in November 2024 and September 2025 respectively. This provided significant oversight of the IAT and associated changes.

So we take the feedback from the Ombudsman seriously. On this point, as I've put in the letter that we put in response to the draft Ombudsman's report, we respectfully disagree and we don't accept that characterisation of the testing of the algorithm, the IAT and the implementation.
witness_organisation: Department of Health, Disability and Ageing
witness_position: Secretary

agency: Department of Health, Disability and Ageing
text: Thank you so—

agency: Department of Health, Disability and Ageing
text: Chair, can I ask another question given the long answer that Mr Comley has just given me in relation to this line of questioning?

agency: Department of Health, Disability and Ageing
text: Sure.

agency: Department of Health, Disability and Ageing
text: We've heard evidence during our Support at Home inquiries, and particularly in relation to the IAT, that the tool as it currently stands doesn't adequately take into account things like cognition, medication management, social issues, toileting, carer profile, psychological issues, physical and personal health and frailty. We've heard from functional assessment experts that these are critical domains, yet in the way the algorithm is designed and to the extent that we have been able to understand it—noting that the Ombudsman says it's still a bit of a black box—they come in so late in the decision-making tree that at best they move people up one or two levels, whereas what functional assessment experts are saying is they should be at the front of the algorithm so that the questions people are being asked at the start of the algorithm throw them basically to the top or the bottom of the tree. All of these things that are really critical for understanding older people's needs come in so late that they can hardly shift people. How is it appropriate for cognitive issues to exist in the test as a secondary consideration rather than a primary one when functional experts are telling us that is not right?

agency: Department of Health, Disability and Ageing
text: Senator Allman-Payne, that can be addressed. The government will consider and finalise terms of reference for the review that it has announced in terms of the classification algorithm and the priority algorithm. The points that you go to are particularly relevant to the classification algorithm and the involvement of experts in that review.
witness_organisation: National Health and Medical Research Council
witness_position: Deputy Secretary, Ageing and Aged Care Group

agency: Department of Health, Disability and Ageing
text: To supplement Ms Stewart's response, as the government has announced, there will be the independent review of the aged-care classification and prioritisation algorithms. We're making sure, as we should, that we ground that review in clinical expertise. We will have an expert advisory group that will bring together experts in gerontology, First Nations, culturally and linguistically diverse groups, allied health and, to your point, dementia care. We have heard that feedback. We have worked with Dementia Australia and other peak bodies around hearing their concerns, and we will be making sure that this is incorporated in that review—for which the terms of reference will be made publicly available in the not too distant future.
witness_organisation: National Health and Medical Research Council
witness_position: First Assistant Secretary, Home Care Division

agency: Department of Health, Disability and Ageing
text: With that answer in mind, I want to come back to my original question. Given that you've just said to me how extensive the concerns are that have been raised by providers, assessors, families, peak bodies and gerontologists, how can you have confidence that the integrated assessment tool is accurately assessing older people right now, particularly those with cognitive issues?

agency: Department of Health, Disability and Ageing
text: The reason I have the confidence is that the integrated assessment tool is the clinical tool that is used, and then what we're talking about are the algorithms. I have a lot of confidence in the tool that was—
witness_organisation: National Health and Medical Research Council
witness_position: Deputy Secretary, Ageing and Aged Care Group

agency: Department of Health, Disability and Ageing
text: Do you have confidence in the algorithm?

agency: Department of Health, Disability and Ageing
text: The confidence in the algorithm—the government has announced its review to do that.
witness_organisation: National Health and Medical Research Council
witness_position: Deputy Secretary, Ageing and Aged Care Group

agency: Department of Health, Disability and Ageing
text: Doesn't that mean you don't have confidence right now; hence why we need a review?

agency: Department of Health, Disability and Ageing
text: I have confidence the algorithm is—
witness_organisation: Department of Health, Disability and Ageing
witness_position: Secretary

agency: Department of Health, Disability and Ageing
text: Let's—

agency: Department of Health, Disability and Ageing
text: Could I just get the answer to the question, please, Chair?

agency: Department of Health, Disability and Ageing
text: If everybody could just hold on for a minute, we will go to the officials at the table for the answer to the question.

agency: Department of Health, Disability and Ageing
text: We have confidence in the algorithm being well tested—reflecting people's needs on the integrated assessment tool. That is not to say we can't go through a process of continuous improvement. One of the things that has happened with the integrated assessment tool is the number of people appealing the outcome has actually been very small.
witness_organisation: National Health and Medical Research Council
witness_position: First Assistant Secretary, Home Care Division

agency: Department of Health, Disability and Ageing
text: It's 0.6 per cent.
witness_organisation: National Health and Medical Research Council
witness_position: Deputy Secretary, Ageing and Aged Care Group

agency: Department of Health, Disability and Ageing
text: Yes, 0.6 per cent have appealed against the decision of the integrated assessment tool—from expert input from assessors. So we have a high degree of confidence in that, notwithstanding the fact that we think continuous improvement is possible. I think it's important to draw a distinction between the prioritisation algorithm and the IAT and the algorithms associated with that. The government earlier on announced a rapid review of the prioritisation algorithm. I think that did reflect the fact that the prioritisation algorithm had too few criteria and was not accurately reflecting some of the needs on prioritisation. So that is the one we've done the rapid review for. We'll now be also reviewing the IAT, but we have a high degree of confidence that the IAT on the classification side is doing a good job of determining need. We acknowledge that external parties have views and we're really keen to engage with them further as we go through the review process to ensure we can continue to refine a mechanism that is being used to allocate a very large number of packages.
witness_organisation: Department of Health, Disability and Ageing
witness_position: Secretary

agency: Department of Health, Disability and Ageing
text: Thank you.

agency: Department of Health, Disability and Ageing
text: Senator Ruston.

agency: Department of Health, Disability and Ageing
text: In response to recommendation 1—or in your response to the Ombudsman, Mr Comley, on 2 November, which was 13 days before the Senate voted on the escalation pathway, or schedule 4 of the amendment to the bill—

agency: Department of Health, Disability and Ageing
text: It was 2 October.

agency: Department of Health, Disability and Ageing
text: Sorry. You said 2 November?
witness_organisation: Department of Health, Disability and Ageing
witness_position: Secretary

agency: Department of Health, Disability and Ageing
text: It was 2 October, sorry. If I said November, I misspoke; 2 November hasn't come yet. During the bill, we had a very short committee within the department. Given that you said that you sought the advice of the Ombudsman to be able to provide the draft recommendations to the ministers throughout the period of it being in draft format, at any time, did you or the ministers' offices seek an agreement from the Ombudsman as to whether it would be appropriate, given the nature of the amendment in schedule 4 to that bill, to at least share in part the relevant recommendations of the Ombudsman's report with the people that were about to vote on this bill?

agency: Department of Health, Disability and Ageing
text: Senator, I want to be clear. I think I corrected my evidence to say that—I originally said we needed the approval of the Ombudsman to put it to the ministers.
witness_organisation: Department of Health, Disability and Ageing
witness_position: Secretary

agency: Department of Health, Disability and Ageing

agency: Department of Health, Disability and Ageing

witness_organisation: Department of Health, Disability and Ageing
witness_position: Secretary

agency: Department of Health, Disability and Ageing

Did you ever seek to provide a level of transparency around this particular issue during those negotiations, given that particularly recommendation 1 and recommendation 4 go to the process that surrounded the schedule 4 amendment to the aged-care Aboriginal and Torres Strait Islander Commissioner bill?

agency: Department of Health, Disability and Ageing
text: We didn't, and it was because it was a draft ombudsman's report.
witness_organisation: Department of Health, Disability and Ageing
witness_position: Secretary

agency: Department of Health, Disability and Ageing

agency: Department of Health, Disability and Ageing

That was a draft report in the same way the ANAO, when they have these reports, provide to the relevant agency a document to allow them to provide any comment, including for factual inaccuracies. It is not common at all for that to go outside government.
witness_organisation: Department of Health, Disability and Ageing
witness_position: Secretary

agency: Department of Health, Disability and Ageing
text: No, and I'm not suggesting that normally it would be common to go outside of government. But before us at the Senate we had an inquiry, a bill and an amendment to a bill that went to the very nature of the concerns that were raised by the Ombudsman in that draft report. So at no time, you're telling me, did you think that the information that was contained in that report, particularly recommendations 1 and 4, were relevant to the extent that the Senate should have been aware of them before they were asked to vote on something, when only a matter of minutes later the Ombudsman's report dropped? Now we find out that something that was very relevant was kept from the Senate—kept from the very workings of the institution of this parliament. You're telling me you never thought to even seek to have that information made available to us?

agency: Department of Health, Disability and Ageing
text: What I endeavoured to do, and what the department endeavoured to do, was assist the Ombudsman by providing responses to the draft report to allow the Ombudsman to finalise their report and for the Ombudsman to then have the opportunity to consider our comments and decide to what extent they would take them into account before finalising the report. witness_organisation: Department of Health, Disability and Ageing
witness_position: Secretary

agency: Department of Health, Disability and Ageing
text: So you sought to assist the Ombudsman, but at no time did you think to assist the parliament in its transparency of deliberations about something that was before it?

agency: Department of Health, Disability and Ageing

witness_organisation: Department of Health, Disability and Ageing
witness_position: Secretary

Did you not think it prudent to advise the government or did you advise the government that maybe it would be prudent to wait to do this until the November sittings so that the Ombudsman's final report could have been transparently seen and ventilated in the context of negotiation in relation to that amendment?

agency: Department of Health, Disability and Ageing

witness_organisation: Department of Health, Disability and Ageing
witness_position: Secretary

agency: Department of Health, Disability and Ageing

Did your government ever consider the merits of allowing the Ombudsman's view to be seen prior to forcing this through the Senate and in effect misleading the Senate by the exclusion of very relevant information in relation to the amendment to the bill that was before the Senate two weeks ago?

agency: Department of Health, Disability and Ageing
text: Senator Ruston, the way you put that question to me, and indeed I think your questions to Mr Comley, misunderstand the relationship between a government and a department to the Ombudsman. The Ombudsman has wide powers to inquire into matters of government administration. The Ombudsman uses those powers, and the Ombudsman makes their own decisions about information that is released to the public and to the parliament. The responsibility of the department, as Mr Comley has explained to you in his evidence just now, is to provide information to the Ombudsman as requested. It's also to support the parliament by providing explanations about the work of the department. It would be wrong to assert that the responsibility of the department is to provide explanations to the parliament about the work of the Ombudsman—

agency: Department of Health, Disability and Ageing
text: Maybe it's your responsibility—

agency: Department of Health, Disability and Ageing
text: and, indeed, if you have questions about the work of the Ombudsman, you probably should direct them to that person.

agency: Department of Health, Disability and Ageing
text: I have no questions in relation to the work of the Ombudsman. Maybe I could ask you both: do you think that the advice of the Ombudsman was relevant to the decisions in relation to amendments to schedule 4?

agency: Department of Health, Disability and Ageing
text: The department has provided a response to the Ombudsman's report and indicated that they had accepted the advice. As that response indicates, we're in the process of implementing many of the recommendations provided by the Ombudsman.

agency: Department of Health, Disability and Ageing
text: I've asked a simple question.

agency: Department of Health, Disability and Ageing
text: I'd also say that I don't think, Senator Ruston, there is a single time that the Ombudsman has provided a draft report to parliament. If you can identify such a time, you should name it.

agency: Department of Health, Disability and Ageing
text: Minister, I asked you a very simple question. agency: Department of Health, Disability and Ageing
text: I note, though, that the demand is foreseeable. I mean, we've known for a really long time that we've got an ageing population, so maybe this is a question for the minister. Minister, given that the recommendation of the royal commission was to stop rationing care, is that the government's view that MSOs are compatible with an unrationed rights-based system?

agency: Department of Health, Disability and Ageing
text: I think you know that the government is making a very large financial investment in aged care to meet the unprecedented growth in demand that arises because of our ageing population. We accept that we need to address that demand. I think the estimates are that by 30 June 2027, 420,000 older people will have access to Support at Home. That's almost triple where it was in 2020. That is a very significant level of growth in that period of time. We're increasing resources substantially, and we're aware that the royal commission pointed to a very extended period of neglect in the aged-care system. We're providing resources to respond to that.

agency: Department of Health, Disability and Ageing
text: It's true, though, isn't it, that this is about government decisions. We've had an instance, for example, where you could put a tax on gas, which would mean that big corporations would pay more so more older people can get care. I guess what I'm trying to get a sense of is that the government's view that in a situation where more and more older people are going to require care, they should just expect further and further rationing, rather than the government looking for revenue streams that would actually meet the needs of the older people who need the care. What we're seeing is increased rationing. We had a ration system. Now we've got MSOs. We're now hearing that that's basically a structural feature. Is this not actually moving further and further away from not rationing care?

One of the things that we do is to try to make plain English and also acknowledge that there are people whose language is not English as their primary language. We have done a whole range of different communications. Some of the ones that we receive very positive feedback about are the older person's voice themselves, particularly through videos and sharing their experiences of how they navigated and went through the system.

To your point about our website and our presence, we've also received feedback that it is difficult to navigate, particularly if people just want to ask a question using artificial intelligence or other prompts that they might use. So we're making that easier for people to be assisted in that way. The other thing I would say is that we listen very carefully to the council of elders, a group that inform the minister on the operations of the act. From time to time, and as often as we can, we run communication material past them to get their views, noting that they represent a very diverse group of older people across Australia. The reason we were nodding is that we do hear that feedback. It's one of those balances around something which is very complex and very large, and making it in plain language.

The final thing I would say is that this morning we were asked a question around communication that we're taking—a communication campaign about aged care. This is about getting people ready and thinking about the aged-care system because very often they come into the system at a point of crisis, when something has happened to them, their family or their kin. We are not yet 12 months in, but we recognise that, as has been described in evidence today, we need to be responsive in some instances. We have already made pragmatic changes where it made sense to do so. We encourage providers to continue to share their thoughts with the department. In fact, we met with a number of key assistive tech and home modification providers, assessors and other interested parties for a full-day workshop a number of months ago, just to make sure that we were taking the time out to say, 'What are you seeing on the ground? What does that look like?' That will complement things we hear either from providers directly or through ministerial correspondence. We are definitely having a look at that. Mr Maldon has mentioned that the evaluation of the program is another part of that key piece about what other people are seeing as well. In respect of crutches specifically, we had heard—not just from the speech you referenced, Senator—some concerns from both providers and older people about the role of prescriptions in respect of assistive technology. We have made it really clear in our assistive technology and home modifications list that they are advisory categories. For example, although some clients or older people may benefit from consultation with an OT, a prescription is not mandatory for things like crutches. We have been trying to make sure that we're enforcing that message when we're engaging more broadly: that there is some guidance here but it's not mandatory.
witness_organisation: National Health and Medical Research Council
witness_position: Assistant Secretary, Home Care Division

agency: Department of Health, Disability and Ageing
text: Is it the case—this has been raised in some of the inquiries that we've had—that the department is looking at situations where, for example, if a medical professional, be they an allied health professional or a doctor, says that somebody needs something, they can get it? We're hearing from podiatrists that there's this backwards and forwards and extra layers of getting approval to be associated providers. I would have thought that if you are a podiatrist you are a podiatrist. Are you looking at getting rid of some of what seem like really clunky bureaucratic barriers to people getting timely and less costly care?

agency: Department of Health, Disability and Ageing
text: That's another area in particular that we are looking at—that associated provider piece. It's being raised by sole traders and by providers; so, yes.
witness_organisation: National Health and Medical Research Council
witness_position: Assistant Secretary, Home Care Division

agency: Department of Health, Disability and Ageing
text: As Ms Snow said, we are taking on board the feedback from the associated providers. I do acknowledge that it was a process to get registration for these associated providers. We thought it was a very important part of the system, given that people are going into older people's homes and into their communities, to have them registered. That was a big implementation task, and I acknowledge that associated providers have had to go through that process. We see this not as an ongoing burden; it is more like an implementation. The other aspect of this is around pricing—assurance on the pricing and checking the pricing. We take that very seriously and have done work on that pricing. I acknowledge that the Aged Care Quality and Safety Commissioner is in the room, and the Complaints Commissioner. We are also taking very seriously the transparency of the pricing and the level of the pricing. I wanted to explain that some of the associated provider issues would be around that, but we are also taking that pricing matter very seriously.
witness_organisation: National Health and Medical Research Council
witness_position: Deputy Secretary, Ageing and Aged Care Group

agency: Department of Health, Disability and Ageing
text: The feedback from the associated providers was very specifically around associated providers that are already accredited health professionals, particularly in the allied health space. I think the view is that if people have been accredited by AHPRA, it would be like asking a doctor to go and get another accreditation to do a home visit. I think that's where the concerns lie. I might go to the inspector. Ms Siegel-Brown had indicated that the office of the inspector was doing some work around looking at ways that the system can be frontloaded so that the money that is being expended is being expended on more timely access to early supports. I am wondering if it is possible for you to give us an update on where that work is at.

agency: Department of Health, Disability and Ageing
text: We have released recently a report called Before the fall, produced by Professor David Cullen, which draws together a lot of evidence around prevention, and the value of front-end loading, as you expressed it, the expenditure to keep people at home for as long as possible and contribute to delaying entry into residential aged care. We are doing some more work around that. We expect to have some preliminary results of that work early next year, probably by the end of January—more modelling around the preventive investment and the difference that might make. We don't have anything further at the moment.
witness_organisation: Inspector-General of Aged Care
witness_position: Acting Inspector-General, Office of the Inspector-General of Aged Care

agency: Department of Health, Disability and Ageing
text: I have a question around the increasing prevalence of the minimum service offers. We are seeing that, increasingly, people are getting a lower level of care than what they've been assessed for. As we've heard, some people are waiting for up to four months to get that. I am wondering whether you have any observations, particularly in relation to that, as it pertains to the recommendations of the royal commission to stop rationing care and to get people care at the point that they need it.

agency: Department of Health, Disability and Ageing
text: As I am sure you are aware, Senator, we recently announced the commencement of the review into the implementation of the 148 recommendations. Our report is due by 1 November 2027. Clearly, the issues that you have just raised will be part of that consideration. I am aware, both from discussions with the department and from the feedback that we get from the many people I am speaking to, as I work my way into this role, that minimum service offers are causing people concern, and they feel uncertain about expending money from their package, because they're not sure when they are going to get the rest of it, and they are worried about budgeting and those kinds of issues. They are the kinds of things people have said to me in the time I've been here. We certainly share their concerns and can imagine that it does introduce uncertainty for individuals. Yes, it's certainly an issue that we're keeping a close eye on.
witness_organisation: Inspector-General of Aged Care
witness_position: Acting Inspector-General, Office of the Inspector-General of Aged Care

agency: Department of Health, Disability and Ageing
text: Thanks, Ms Pope. I am conscious that you have only been in the role for a short time. Are there any other issues that are being raised, that are bubbling to the surface, that are on your radar at the moment?

agency: Department of Health, Disability and Ageing
text: Yes. They probably won't surprise you, because I am sure they are things that you are hearing as well: access to services under Support at Home; finding sufficient providers able to respond to requests for services; and transitioning from CHSP to Support at Home. It's a new system and people are still finding that challenging. There are concerns about the future of CHSP—welcoming the extension, but wanting to understand what it will look like in the future. There is welcoming of certainty now, but what's to come in the future? There are concerns around transparency of costs, such as the examples you were talking about. It is about understanding what it means to be charged a certain amount and then what that will turn into, in terms of what gets charged to the package, and how they budget for and manage those things. They're probably the main concerns. It is about getting used to the new system, working out how to access it, a bit of concern around complexity of information and how to access information, and needing help to work their way through understanding the advice they're being given and how to go about it.
witness_organisation: Inspector-General of Aged Care
witness_position: Acting Inspector-General, Office of the Inspector-General of Aged Care

agency: Department of Health, Disability and Ageing

agency: Department of Health, Disability and Ageing

agency: Department of Health, Disability and Ageing
text: It was $1.4 billion. There are a few steps here. There are two primary components of that. One was Support at Home and the other was Residential Aged Care. I'll leave Residential Aged Care out of it, for the time being. There is a difference between what was in the Final Budget Outcome and what was in our annual report. That came out yesterday. The difference is around $200 million. Our annual report shows about a $1.2 billion underspend across the aged-care services program. In relation to Support at Home, $727 million worth is the component that relates to Support at Home.
witness_organisation: National Health and Medical Research Council
witness_position: First Assistant Secretary, Home Care Division

agency: Department of Health, Disability and Ageing

agency: Department of Health, Disability and Ageing
text: It is 2025-26. That would be Support at Home. That's from 1 November to 30 June 2026. There are a couple of reasons. Utilisation is one of the reasons that we have talked about. We also know that there were an additional 83,000 places released into the system—20,000 in the lead-up to 1 November, 20,000 in the period between 1 November and 31 December, and 43,000 from 1 January to 30 June 2026. Our analysis shows that a large portion of that has been the ability of those 83,000 places to be absorbed. There's no deliberate intention of anyone to underspend. agency: Department of Health, Disability and Ageing
text: Your contention is that the lion's share of the reason for the lack of utilisation of packages is the inability of the sector to be able to provide the services that people want, not that there's been any other behavioural change.
