witness_position: First Assistant Secretary, Home Care Division

agency: Department of Health, Disability and Ageing

At no time have I heard anything come out of your mouth to suggest that there are any potential structural changes that have occurred within how people are receiving their care in the home that may be contributing to their utilisation of packages. My question to you is: have you, at any time over the period that Support at Home has been in operation, sought to find out what those contributing factors are in any way that can be validated?

agency: Department of Health, Disability and Ageing
text: In terms of Mr Pugh's response to the question, I do acknowledge the perception of yours that he was blaming others, but that's not the intent; it was around the actual market conditions. We are very aware that this is a brand-new program and we're not one year in. We have been getting thousands of people across to the program, getting new service agreements done, communicating clearly about the changes that are happening, getting people in who were grandfathered—a number of people were grandfathered—and also getting ready in terms of co-contributions. There was work and learnings for us—and I acknowledge Liz Hefren-Webb from the commission—around pricing transparency and actions that the department and the commission undertook together to ensure that older people had that transparency around the prices in their local area and providers putting that on to the system. There were a number of factors that contributed to that.
witness_organisation: National Health and Medical Research Council
witness_position: Deputy Secretary, Ageing and Aged Care Group

agency: Department of Health, Disability and Ageing
text: Can I just say, Senator, we are expending a lot of effort on this question of utilisation and what's driving it. It's a very important factor because we want people to access the services but we also need to understand from a forward-looking perspective whether the level of utilisation that we're seeing is a permanent or a transitional factor. It's very important in terms of the overall program. There's probably a third factor that Mr Pugh didn't mention, which is that we see an observed behaviour. Whenever you give someone a package, it takes them a while to ramp up to their full service offering. That's not necessarily about availability of workforce; it's also about literally just finding the right providers and working out what works for you. That takes time. We see higher utilisation, for example, in the second quarter of someone having a package than in the first quarter, on a consistent basis. We have been engaging with the sector. We've been talking to them to explain what they think is driving the lags, and we're putting in a lot of effort to try and understand what is the balance between these three drivers that we've identified and what is likely to drive utilisation. A particular part of that last bit is that, because of the significant uptick in the number of packages, the proportion of packages that are brand-new, versus existing rolled-over packages, is higher than it was previously. As we move to this financial year, the ratio of new packages to existing packages will be lower and we have to understand that for the purposes of forecasting.

witness_position: Secretary

agency: Department of Health, Disability and Ageing

agency: Department of Health, Disability and Ageing

I have a few things in response to some of the things that you've all just put on the record. You made the comment that it takes people a while to ramp up and it's usually the second quarter when you start seeing a more normal use of utilisation. Of course, we don't want to see older Australians paying any more than they need to, but, at the end of the day, they won't be paying anything at all if there isn't a sector there that is viable, in order to be able to provide these services.

We're hearing very dire stories. The information that you've provided to me gives me no confidence that you're on top of the numbers as yet, because you've taken so much on. text: The budget for 2026-27 for the Transition Care Program is $454.5 million. The way the transition care works is that a number of places are funded. The Hospital to Aged Care Dementia Support Program puts a service around them to support their transition and to support when they go into residential care, to support the planning and care for them to more easily transition to a new care setting.

text: That's great. Yes, there has been a lot of feedback about the RACPA, and I have to say that some of it has been fairly toxic. agency: Department of Health, Disability and Ageing
text:
I may not have any staff, but I have a lot of friends who like to work with me. I'll just go through, at a very high level, how the price was built because, yes, as part of the price build, we did make an assessment of the administration costs for 2025-26. Earlier, you raised the issue of using data from 2023-24 and indexing it forward. We start the price build by using the most recent year of complete data, and the most recent year of complete data that we had through the Aged Care Financial Report was 2023-24. We then adjust that for multiple data sources. In the case of this year's price, page 7 of the RACPA, which we put on the internet, has some 26 data sources, including the ACFR and not one but five Fair Work Commission decisions.

We look at all the costs that are in the ACFR and adjust them for all of those data recognitions. Then, to index them forward, we use a combination of three different indexes. For the Hansard, I'll read them in, in detail. We use an adjusted version of the Australian Bureau of Statistics total hourly rates of pay, excluding bonuses, for private healthcare and social assistance wage price indexes. We also use detail from the Fair Work Commission Annual Wage Review Decision and the Reserve Bank of Australia wage price forecast to estimate future wage growth. Then we index forward non-labour costs, such as administration, using the consumer price index subgroups. So we use the best data and the best indices that we've got from agencies outside IHACPA to project what the costs are going to be going forward.

I think there are a couple of special things about this price that are worth just touching on, partly because credit is due to the providers over the one that had the biggest impact. The difference in costs between 2022-23 and 2023-24 is because, between those two years, we saw a dramatic reduction in the use of agency staff, such as agency nurses and locums, in residential care. As you know, HR accounts for around 80 per cent of the costs of these facilities, so reducing their costs by reducing their use of such staff has had a long-term impact on how we assess the costs and project them forward. An agency nurse will cost anywhere between two and five times what a permanent employee will cost.
witness_organisation: Independent Health and Aged Care Pricing Authority
witness_position: Chief Executive Officer

agency: Department of Health, Disability and Ageing
text: You're saying that was from 2022-23 to 2023-24?

agency: Department of Health, Disability and Ageing
text: Yes. Everyone expects wages costs everywhere to go up year on year but, between 2022-23 and 2023-24, we saw those costs come down because of the significant reduction in the use of agency staff.
witness_organisation: Independent Health and Aged Care Pricing Authority
witness_position: Chief Executive Officer

agency: Department of Health, Disability and Ageing
text: You were using 2023-24 data, though, weren't you?

agency: Department of Health, Disability and Ageing
text:
Yes. But that use of permanent staff instead of agency staff has remained consistent and been maintained. All credit to the providers, because that's a far more efficient and, as would be agreed by my colleagues from safety and quality, far safer employment model. It might have had something to do with the significant increases coming out of the Fair Work Commission's decisions, which the government funded, that made permanent employment in residential care more attractive than it had been previously. But, notwithstanding why it happened, it happened. So indexing that forward got us to a smaller increase than in the previous year; in the reference year of 2022-23, we were still seeing those higher labour costs. The other thing that's worth noting is, yes, while there are significant Fair Work Australia decisions that impact on this year's price, a lot of them, in part, were worked into the price last year, so some of them were already locked in and loaded. So it's not just a translation of 4.5 per cent on last year's price. We've built the price new, as we do every year, and that mitigates any risks of underpayment or overpayment. Also, we've looked at the costs against all of those data sources, including Fair Work Commission decisions.

I have sympathy for the providers who looked at that increase and at what they were expecting to come down the pipe, but this is how the government's direction from way back in August 2022 directs us to cast the price, which is to use actual costs of care—not projected but actual, so we have to use, in effect, historical data—and build the price by using the same approaches that we use for hospitals. So that's what we do. The only difference between the two models is that, in hospitals, we've got 40 years of cost data, so we can build our own index, which is very reliable. In the case of aged care, we're only starting to collect that data, so we use multiple indices from the ABS, the Fair Work Commission and the Reserve Bank of Australia.
witness_organisation: Independent Health and Aged Care Pricing Authority
witness_position: Chief Executive Officer

agency: Department of Health, Disability and Ageing
text: I accept the quite extensive way you go about reaching your determination in relation to the price increase that you obviously recommend to government in relation to AN-ACC. From the layman's perspective, given the hyperinflationary environment that we're in at the moment, the 4.75 per cent pay increase that we saw from the Fair Work Commission and a lot of the challenges of change that's occurred in the sector, I'm just interested—I mean, 2.55 per cent did seem a very low number to be recommending, to be fair, particularly with, as I said, 4.75 per cent. Where could I send somebody from the sector who raises this issue of the inadequacy of the 2.55 per cent for them to actually find a level of transparency about the methodology, calculations et cetera that you've used to get to that point so that they can better understand how you got there? Is there a place where somebody could get that information?

agency: Department of Health, Disability and Ageing
text:
Actually, I'll take full responsibility for that. As you know, we put everything on the website—our technical specifications, the pricing frameworks, the actual pricing advice. It's all there in all of its mathematical glory, but, if you're running a resident-care facility, you're not going to have time to spend the eight or nine hours to digest all of that. It's also written by analysts and statisticians, so it's not in a language that you would say is very accessible. I haven't done my job, I think, in providing a more accessible communication. Yes, we put it out on LinkedIn and all that sort of stuff, but we've got to get better, in fact, in similar terms to the way that I just walked you through how the price was built, with a bit more detail in it so people can see what is in the pricing advice we give to government but also what's not.

The most regular exchange that we have with StewartBrown is that StewartBrown always want to raise the issue of margin, and we are compelled by government direction to provide pricing advice built on actual costs. Profit margin isn't a cost; it's something you generate through efficiency or through increased revenue. We can't build a margin into a price, because that's not driven by the actual operational costs. StewartBrown say that, without a margin, they won't have money for bills on presentation, expansion, investment and all of those things. They are all very valid concerns, but our component is very much boxed into providing that cost based price advice. Now, if anyone wants to have a conversation or be walked through that process, or if they've got specific issues, in addition to the four or five times a year that we put things out for comment and engagement, they can email me or they can email the inquiries mailbox. In fact, a couple have. When we've talked them through how the price was built, they've understood it. They've not been happy about it, but they've still understood why the numbers come out the way they come out. Now—
witness_organisation: Independent Health and Aged Care Pricing Authority
witness_position: Chief Executive Officer

agency: Department of Health, Disability and Ageing
text:
You say they understood but they're not happy about it. It's one thing to understand the methodology that you apply to it. It's another one to agree that that is the right methodology. If you walked me through it, I could probably understand how you reach the number that you reach. It strikes me that this issue is far greater than not having margin built into the number. Most people who've spoken to me are suggesting that they will actually have to take action because of the impact on their potential viability. It also, to a large degree, almost makes the minister's comments around the extra 5,000 beds that he thinks that the sector's going to go and build on the back of his investment in the budget—that these changes basically negate all of the uplift that was proposed by that.

You say you started off with the 2023-24 average costings. What indexation factors were applied? Obviously you apply them to wages, superannuation, CPI, fair work et cetera. Do you actually provide advice about, of the 2.55 per cent increase that you've recommended, how much is attributed to each of those indexation factors? Is there a level of transparency about what factors are having the largest or smallest amount of impact or contribution on changes?

agency: Department of Health, Disability and Ageing
text: It is very transparent to a point, but there comes a point where you're dismantling the bike so that it's not rideable anymore. Trying to disaggregate specific non-care-related administration costs is actually very complex because that's not the way the data is recorded at the business end. We've got to use the way the data is recorded to build the price. We've actually worked with aged-care providers over the last couple of years on a particular issue around time spent away from the residence as being not all active administrative time. Sometimes they're asleep. In the first round, we were probably overcounting that time, and we worked with providers to correct it. The only way that we can learn and improve the price—and we're an organisation that is very much dedicated to improving what we do on an annual basis, is both to get that direct feedback at IHACPA and, where there are serious viability issues, to feed that through to the department so that they can raise it with us and we can look at what it is that is not being met. What is the specific element of funding? Is it workforce? Well, because of the way that we calculate the workforce costs, we're actually pretty confident about that. Is that admin? Is it insurance? Is it something else that we're not capturing or isn't in the ACFR but we need to take account of? As a last resort because I understand how busy providers are, do we need to ask for additional data from them? As I said, it's a last resort because we know that many of them struggle to maintain their existing data commitments.

It's a much bigger question than you think. I've got some perspective on that, having run a few hospitals, including in Tasmania. The costs of them really relate to the patient themselves. You can make some sweeping generalisations about the cost of maintenance care, and that's about $1,200 to $1,500 a day, but, once again, these patients aren't stranded for no reason. Increasingly, it's not as simple as a lack of residential care places for them to go to. That's certainly an element. I'm not disagreeing with that. But, for many of them—and it has come up in the discussion today—their needs are complex to the extent where residential care can't immediately take them. There are programs, like transition care, which provide six weeks support to move people on to their home or residential care, but there are an increasing number of patients for whom that's not sufficient. It's not just dementia, and it's not just what you could categorise as antisocial behaviours—smoking, particular mental disorders, borderline personality disorder and so on. It can be that the patient has multiple chronic conditions—something that is a particular issue in Tasmania—and they actually require a lot of health care support.

We don't quite have a model that will support those sorts of patients yet. In other countries—Senator Roberts was referring to step-down care. That's not where it's gone elsewhere. It's gone into skilled nursing facilities that provide support for these people with complex ongoing needs. We certainly have a large number of them, but we don't have enough of them in any one location to make a facility viable, so we're still exploring all of that.

We'll accept information from a whole range of sources and be carefully weighing up the evidence across nine areas that we've identified as a way of grouping together the recommendations. We'll also be looking at each of the recommendations individually, but we have nine major areas, and that is set out on our website and in the announcement of the review. It's the widest possible range of sources. The agencies we oversee will be providing responses and information to us about the work they have done in relation to each of the recommendations, and we will be testing that against other evidence that we gather. We do a lot of work with stakeholders, and that's really been the focus of my work so far in the role, getting to know the stakeholder environment and working with the very wide range of stakeholders that have a view around aged care. So it's gathering information from every possible source.

agency: Department of Health, Disability and Ageing
text: So this is a cakewalk for you. I've got some questions about access to biologic treatments for children with Crohn's disease. I know we've gone over this a number of times at Senate estimates. I've raised this a number of times at Senate estimates, and I know PBAC has considered it on a number of occasions. We are talking about children with Crohn's disease and other serious inflammatory conditions who are being required to trial medications like methotrexate and high-dose steroids before they can access biologic treatments through the PBS. These are children dealing with debilitating illnesses whose treating specialists are concerned that delaying access to appropriate treatments and access to biologics could cause permanent, irreversible damage. Can you give an update of where we're at and why it is taking so long to actually get a solution.

agency: Department of Health, Disability and Ageing
text: The department and the PBAC acknowledge the severity of inflammatory bowel disease like Crohn's disease and the major impact it has on children and their parents. Since March 2024, the department and the Pharmaceutical Benefits Advisory Committee have been working with clinicians and patient representatives to ensure the PBS criteria for inflammatory bowel disease reflect contemporary clinical practice. There have been a range of recommendations made by the PBAC since December 2024, and I could step through the changes in the implementation of those if that's helpful or provide them on notice.
witness_organisation: National Health and Medical Research Council
witness_position: Assistant Secretary, Technology Assessment and Access Division

agency: Department of Health, Disability and Ageing
text: Maybe you could provide them on notice. How far away are we from actually getting this resolved?

agency: Department of Health, Disability and Ageing
text: There are a range of things that have been completed, and then there are some things that are partially completed, but, from December 2024 through to the recommendations in May 2026, we anticipate that they'll be completed by the end of this calendar year. At a high-level summary, the work for Crohn's disease has been complete, and what we haven't completed is the work related to ulcerative colitis, but that should be completed by the end of this calendar year.
witness_organisation: National Health and Medical Research Council
witness_position: Assistant Secretary, Technology Assessment and Access Division

agency: Department of Health, Disability and Ageing
text: We have the deputy chair of the PBAC at the table, and I want to just defer to her. There's been a lot of work, as Mr Rintoul has said, on really trying to resolve some of the issues that we've talked about at previous hearings. So it might be helpful if Professor Watson can give an update as well.
witness_organisation: Department of Health, Disability and Ageing
witness_position: First Assistant Secretary, Technology Assessment and Access Division

agency: Department of Health, Disability and Ageing

Why is this taking so long? It seems like there's a clear issue and a very clear potential solution: actually allowing health practitioners to use a bit more discretion. Why haven't we landed there yet? Why is it taking so long?

agency: Department of Health, Disability and Ageing
text: I think Mr Rintoul had started to go there. We have implemented changes for paediatric patients with severe to moderate Crohn's disease, and that was done in October, and then we're on track to broaden changes for patients with ulcerative colitis. witness_position: First Assistant Secretary, Technology Assessment and Access Division

agency: Department of Health, Disability and Ageing

Why haven't we moved to discretion, as we do with so many—

agency: Department of Health, Disability and Ageing
text: I might see if the Chief Medical Officer can give some advice on this.

witness_position: First Assistant Secretary, Technology Assessment and Access Division

agency: Department of Health, Disability and Ageing
text: Why can't we give treating specialists greater discretion to make these decisions based on the clinical needs of the child in front of them, as we do for a bunch of drugs?

agency: Department of Health, Disability and Ageing
text: Senator, as you know, prescribing decisions are a decision for each of the treating specialists to make with the patient and their family. But I think the issue you're getting to is about the cost of these treatments if the specialist is prescribing outside of the PBS; is that correct?
witness_organisation: Department of Health, Disability and Ageing
witness_position: Chief Medical Officer

agency: Department of Health, Disability and Ageing
text: Professor, my understanding is that a bunch of these are now off patent and that there are alternatives, so it's not like these are hugely costly experimental drugs.

agency: Department of Health, Disability and Ageing
text: They're expensive treatments if they are purchased privately. That's correct.
witness_organisation: Department of Health, Disability and Ageing
witness_position: Chief Medical Officer

agency: Department of Health, Disability and Ageing
text: I hope Professor Watson doesn't mind me throwing to her, because there has been a lot of consideration in terms of when for first line and second line as part of the PBAC discussion. Are you happy for me to throw to you, Professor Watson?
witness_organisation: Department of Health, Disability and Ageing
witness_position: Deputy Secretary, Systems Strategy Group

agency: Department of Health, Disability and Ageing
text: Since 2024, PBAC has been working closely with the clinical experts through their craft group, GESA, and through Crohn's and Colitis Australia, the patient network. We've been trying to revisit all the indications and restrictions as they have been set in the schedule now for a number of years. There are only two biologics that are actually available at the moment for paediatric use. What we've been trying to do is find ways to open up the prescribing capacity for those two drugs for a population where we've noted urgent clinical need, where we've tried for many years to attract new entries into the market and see sponsors bring forth submissions. PBAC, with the help of our stakeholder groups, has actually attempted to methodically work through these restrictions. They are quite complex because they're across a broad spectrum of disease, not just Crohn's, not just colitis, not just moderate—all the way through to severe and acute. What we've tried to do is make sure that there are no unintended consequences where we are giving discretion to prescribers to prescribe out of indication, that it's going to be on the basis of evidence of safety and effectiveness, that we can ensure our clinicians are working with us and that the guidelines are contemporary and based on guidelines not just here in Australia but also reflect international practice. I think the frustration is well noted about how long this is taking, but there is good intention here to make sure they are best suited and fit for purpose for the Australian clinical setting and also for the age groups across the paediatric spectrum.
witness_organisation: National Health and Medical Research Council
witness_position: Deputy Chair

agency: Department of Health, Disability and Ageing
text: It has taken three years, and Chief Medical Officer said that it's up to the discretion of the doctor, but clearly it's not in this case. Why are there restrictions on use where clearly this is an effective treatment? Are there clinical reasons, or is it a cost thing?

agency: Department of Health, Disability and Ageing
text: I think there are variable reasons. There are reasons in terms of historical legacy. There are reasons in terms of lack of evidence in some age groups and some spectrums of disease. And there are restrictions still in place while we untangle the unintended consequence of delinking and then inadvertently excluding those who are already able to actively be prescribed these because of the acute nature of their disease before we open it up to a whole of population.
witness_organisation: National Health and Medical Research Council
witness_position: Deputy Chair

agency: Department of Health, Disability and Ageing
text: We've recently seen broader PBS access to certain cancer treatments, including some really expensive on-patent medicines, with far greater discretion for treating clinicians. My team brought up the example of Minister Butler announcing the general listing of on-patent cancer treatments worth $5,000-plus per month that provide for clinical discretion. And there's a media release on the PBS website saying a number of low-cost antidepressants have been moved from restricted to unrestricted benefits with eligibility criteria removed. Why do we seem incapable of doing that for these drugs that are affective for children? They don't get those years back, and their parents rightly want access to these treatments.

agency: Department of Health, Disability and Ageing
text: I don't think it's a useful comparison, because the broad-spectrum work that went on for cancer listings was in the presence of new technology for broadening access for very small subtypes of cancer disease and rarer cancers that were never going to see submissions come forward. There's something quite different going on here. If you like, we're trying to do a catch up for paediatric access in the presence of years where paediatrics has actually been ignored across many diseases and conditions. With good faith, the stakeholders and the committee and the department are trying to undo this legacy of a forgotten area of a population, where sponsors are just not commercially enticed to do a lot of work in the paediatric populations across multiple areas.
witness_organisation: National Health and Medical Research Council
witness_position: Deputy Chair

agency: Department of Health, Disability and Ageing
text: And I really appreciate your work on this, but to come back to the patients that want access to this—children, who don't get these years back—in the absence of this decision they are being forced to go through all sorts of treatments which can leave permanent damage, lifelong side effects that they have to deal with. Can you give us a timeline? Surely there's something that can be done to expedite this process?

agency: Department of Health, Disability and Ageing
text: There's a commitment that can be seen in the public summary documents to this being an evolving piece of work. While recommendations and advice have been provided to government and to the department, that work is ongoing and due for implementation in the very near future. The future work of PBAC itself continues in a rolling way, and we've invited both sponsors and stakeholders to continue that work with us.
witness_organisation: National Health and Medical Research Council
witness_position: Deputy Chair

agency: Department of Health, Disability and Ageing
text:
I really encourage everyone involved to expedite the work and come up with a solution for people who desperately want access to this.

I have some questions on bulk-billing and bulk-billing clinics. I want to congratulate you for your work on bulk-billing. There are some really encouraging results from what I've seen, and I acknowledge that there's a huge amount of work that's been happening in the department, and the government's obviously been tipping in more money and doing a lot in this space. It looks like New South Wales is nearly at 90 per cent, which is a good result. But, to come a bit closer to home, in the ACT we're still below 60 per cent, and the areas surrounding the ACT are all comfortably above 80 per cent. The bulk-billing rates in north-east suburbs of Sydney like Mosman, Vaucluse, Bondi, Point Piper, Bellevue Hill are higher than the bulk-billing rates here in Canberra. Looking at the stats, other states bulk-bill their non-concession cardholders more than our concession cardholders are bulk-billed. I find that pretty shocking. Nearly a third of Canberrans—30 per cent—have never actually been bulk-billed. So we've seen a tiny increase—I think 2½ per cent; I acknowledge that. On the current trajectory, do we expect the ACT to actually get to the 90 per cent that the Prime Minister has talked about?

agency: Department of Health, Disability and Ageing
text: The bulk-billing incentives that the government have provided incentivise clinics and clinicians to move their clinics to a situation where they bulk-bill all their patients, and through the triple bulk-billing incentive they have the opportunity to get an uplift for their entire business if they accept that. There are specific areas of the country where it's proved to be challenging to incentivise them, based on their ability to find other business models that are effective, and the ACT has been one where that's been a particular challenge. We've been looking at some of those areas and looking at whether there are other ways to encourage those clinics to adopt those. But you're right in saying that the ACT has a lower rate than other parts of the country in accepting those incentives.

agency: Department of Health, Disability and Ageing
text: I keep getting told that if we changed the MMM rating in Canberra it wouldn't do anything. agency: Department of Health, Disability and Ageing
text: The MMM ratings are fixed on statistical definitions that are deliberately set outside those parameters that governments put their thumb on. The circumstances around the ACT mean that other business models have proved to be more attractive here than they are in other parts of the country. In the areas that surround Canberra, where populations are less dense and that have a different make-up, those models have proved effective, and we're seeing a very substantial increase in the rate of bulk-billing across the country. Indeed, the RACGP put out their survey this morning confirming the figures that we have, which show a very substantial increase overall in bulk-billing and a substantial increase in the number of clinics that are doing that. But in the ACT—
witness_organisation: Department of Health, Disability and Ageing
witness_position: First Assistant Secretary, Medicare Benefits and Digital Health Division

agency: Department of Health, Disability and Ageing
text: I acknowledge that, but I'm a senator for the ACT, so I'm really keen to focus on that.

text: These are challenging problems and I appreciate your concern. It's quite understandable. That has tended to be one of the issues that has contributed to these statistics, and we're continuing to look for ways to incentivise practitioners in the ACT to take up the incentives that the government is providing.

text: I appreciate that, but, with respect, we can't be looking that hard if they've gone from 40 per cent to 30 per cent. Is this a market issue? What needs to happen? We have a two-speed economy here. There are a whole bunch of people earning good money and there are so many Canberrans who simply cannot afford to pay for things like ultrasounds. How do we how fix this?

agency: Department of Health, Disability and Ageing
text: We've recently undertaken a women's imaging review, which included ultrasound services and breast imaging. The department has undertaken that in consultation with stakeholders. witness_organisation: Department of Health, Disability and Ageing
witness_position: Assistant Secretary, Medicare Benefits and Digital Health Division

agency: Department of Health, Disability and Ageing

That just seems like price gouging to me. Are there not mechanisms in place where we can force providers to—

agency: Department of Health, Disability and Ageing
text: There's a bulk-billing incentive for imaging. If a patient is bulk-billed, instead of having the service out of hospital, where there's an 85 per cent rebate to the patient, if they're bulk-billed 95 per cent of the fee goes to the provider.
witness_organisation: Department of Health, Disability and Ageing
witness_position: Assistant Secretary, Medicare Benefits and Digital Health Division

agency: Department of Health, Disability and Ageing

agency: Department of Health, Disability and Ageing
text: Once this answer's complete, we'll rotate the call, Senator Pocock.

agency: Department of Health, Disability and Ageing
text: As Ms Warner has pointed out, we've recently done a review in this area. It is certainly an issue where the department continues to work with stakeholders, including those providers, patient groups and others, to try and find a way to incentivise the programs that government has made available to underpin bulk-billing.
witness_organisation: Department of Health, Disability and Ageing
witness_position: First Assistant Secretary, Medicare Benefits and Digital Health Division

agency: Department of Health, Disability and Ageing
text: Okay. I find it totally unacceptable that we have a bulk-billing rate of 30 per cent for ultrasounds in the ACT, and it doesn't sound like there are any sorts of solutions, even on the table, to try and address that. We have all these problems that I keep being told are specific to the ACT, yet we can't solve any. We have so many smart people in this room. Minister, please. I acknowledge the investments the government has made, but we've got to be able to sort this out. Not everyone in Canberra can just stump up the cash every time.

agency: Department of Health, Disability and Ageing
text: No, and I think you've recognised—and thank you for acknowledging it—the investment the government's made in bulk-billing. If there are more interventions that are needed, we'll consider them. As you know, we are working very hard on developing our health workforce as well. I won't go through that, because it's part of the next outcome, but there's a lot of work that this government is doing to train the next generation of health workforce as well, noting that had a pretty steady decline in training over the decade before this government came into power.

agency: Department of Health, Disability and Ageing
text:
In the correspondence that was also provided as part of that same freedom of information request, there appears to be quite an amount of information that has been redacted in relation to the modelling or assessment that has been undertaken by the department in relation to the impact on public hospital admissions as a result of these changes. On 12 May there was a request from the Public Hospital Strategy Branch saying they were 'working on all things public hospital funding'. They said:

After the Minister's press club speech, we've started thinking about how the PHI rebate changes might affect public hospital demand (and overall costs to the Commonwealth/states) for over 65s. We assume some people will drop or downgrade hospital cover, and that this will lead to increased demand in the public sector. So we're keen to get a sense of what demand increase we might expect, so we can work that into our modelling/projections for the next few years. We have a few general and a few specific questions, and would appreciate anything you can provide on these: • How did you estimate how many people might give up their hospital cover as a result of this policy change (we've seen

44000 in the media—is this correct)? How confident is the team in that estimate?

And then it's redacted. The next question is:

• Do you think this cohort will be representative of the broader 65+ cohort, or perhaps different, e.g. skew

wealthier/younger/healthier?

And then it's redacted.

• We noted this report was quoted in the media—do your team think this analysis is valid/appropriate?

And then it's redacted. The only thing that isn't redacted is:

• We heard about an impact analysis piece that would come out this week—is that correct? Are we able to see a copy? Yes

the OIA will publish the impact analysis for the rebate change tomorrow. We will send you a copy …

So, quite clearly, there was concern in your department in regard to the impact on the public hospitals and, therefore, consequentially on the Commonwealth of these changes. You've obviously provided responses to this person who has reached out seeking this information so they're able to model it, but you have redacted it under section 47C of the Freedom of Information Act. I'm keen to give you the opportunity to give me a justification as to why that information was redacted, or perhaps provide me with that information, because I think it is seminal to the implications of a very significant policy decision.

agency: Department of Health, Disability and Ageing
text: I understand that FOI is actually under review in terms of—there's been a review request in relation to that FOI, and that is underway. In terms of how and why things have been redacted, there are a number of reasons why they've been redacted. I don't have the FOI request in front of me, but I think there are a number of clauses that were used from the legislation, in terms of the redaction. So that review is underway and that will provide us with the context for that.
witness_organisation: Department of Health, Disability and Ageing
witness_position: Deputy Secretary, Systems Strategy Group

agency: Department of Health, Disability and Ageing
text: So you're not going to provide me with any additional information? You're still going to—

agency: Department of Health, Disability and Ageing
text: I'm happy to try and answer any specific questions. I don't have the specific FOI or the rationale for each of those individual redactions.
witness_organisation: Department of Health, Disability and Ageing
witness_position: Deputy Secretary, Systems Strategy Group

agency: Department of Health, Disability and Ageing
text: Do you think the cohort will be representative of the broader over-65s cohort, or do you think it will be skewed to the wealthier, younger or healthier, or perhaps to pensioners?

agency: Department of Health, Disability and Ageing
text: I don't know how we've responded to the specific question, but—
witness_organisation: Department of Health, Disability and Ageing
witness_position: Deputy Secretary, Systems Strategy Group

agency: Department of Health, Disability and Ageing

witness_organisation: Department of Health, Disability and Ageing
witness_position: Deputy Secretary, Systems Strategy Group

text: I'd actually like to know what the answer was in here, not some sort of vague extrapolation from you on what you might or might not think it was. I would have thought that it would have made sense to have actually sought this advice before you made the announcement.

agency: Department of Health, Disability and Ageing
text: Both those branches that deal with health insurance and public hospitals work for me. Under budget confidentiality, the totality of information is not always shared. So I would need to go away and look at the timing of where that document relates to. But there were people from my public hospital team that were involved where there were conversations on this measure. Sometimes it could be that a junior officer has seen something and asked a question. That may be what that email refers to there. I'd need to go away and check. But I can tell you, because both those teams work for me, that there were people involved in this measure.
witness_organisation: Department of Health, Disability and Ageing
witness_position: First Assistant Secretary, Portfolio Strategy Division

text:
Subsequent to that email, there was another email on 19 May where the hospital funding, modelling and reform section said:

We've done some thinking around the PHI rebate changes for people aged 65+ and what this might mean for public hospital demand. … The PHI rebate is likely to impact less than 1% of public hospital demand …

That was related to the 2028-29 year. We subsequently know that in the 2029-30 year, they'll be a 77.3 per cent increase in the number of people who drop their cover according to your estimation. Is it possible, maybe in that deliberation overnight, that you could find us some more information on that?

agency: Department of Health, Disability and Ageing

agency: Department of Health, Disability and Ageing
text: Application 1754, surgical procedures for gender affirmation in adults, is to the medical benefits advisory committee. There was a news report on the weekend, titled, 'Plastic surgeons push to fund 30 transgender surgeries on Medicare amid safety concerns'. It's an application by the Australian Association of Plastic Surgeons to have multiple types of transgender surgeries listed on Medicare so they can be performed free of charge to a patient in a public hospital, subject to resource availability. Is this correct?

agency: Department of Health, Disability and Ageing
text: Yes, the Australian Society of Plastic Surgeons has made an application to the Medical Services Advisory Committee for gender-affirming surgeries for adults.
witness_organisation: Department of Health, Disability and Ageing
witness_position: First Assistant Secretary, Technology Assessment and Access Division

agency: Department of Health, Disability and Ageing
text: In effect, if it's successful, this means all taxpayers are paying for these surgeries, whether they agree with transgenderism or not. What will be the annual cost to taxpayers if the application is approved?

agency: Department of Health, Disability and Ageing
text: It's probably important to note that this application is very early in its process. The Medical Services Advisory Committee is meeting again later in November to discuss the clinical efficacy of these surgeries. Then we'd have to get to, in due course, the cost effectiveness. We're a while away from any decisions or recommendations out of the committee, and, ultimately, any recommendations would be a decision of government. We're a long way away from that.
witness_organisation: Department of Health, Disability and Ageing
witness_position: First Assistant Secretary, Technology Assessment and Access Division

agency: Department of Health, Disability and Ageing
text: So there are no cost estimates yet?

agency: Department of Health, Disability and Ageing
text: Not at this stage, no.
witness_organisation: Department of Health, Disability and Ageing
witness_position: First Assistant Secretary, Technology Assessment and Access Division

agency: Department of Health, Disability and Ageing
text: The title of the application includes the phrase 'gender incongruence', which is 'a medical and psychological term defined by the World Health Organisation as a marked and persistent mismatch between an adult's experienced or expressed gender and their assigned sex at birth'. Minister, is this use of 'assigned sex at birth' consistent with departmental language on this issue, or has the applicant jumped ahead of the department's position?

agency: Department of Health, Disability and Ageing
text: Senator, I can't speak for the applicant. I certainly know that there is some medical advice that we can give you about the right terminology in the particular context that you're talking about.

agency: Department of Health, Disability and Ageing
text: Terminology is a good word, Minister, because it's an accurate word. What's happening, according to an article I read in the Weekend Australian, which is the only newspaper I read—

agency: Department of Health, Disability and Ageing
text: Not the Courier Mail?

agency: Department of Health, Disability and Ageing
text: Sometimes. They're about changing the language, which is what a lot of advocates try to do, to make it sweeter and more palatable. They're changing established terms like gender dysphoria and making it 'gender incongruence'. Minister, for clarity, is it the policy of the department of health that sex is not a biological fact but rather is assigned and not determined at birth? Is sex assigned or determined at birth?

agency: Department of Health, Disability and Ageing
text: We can take you through the definitions that are given. I think the most relevant one would be—is it the NHMRC definition? But this is obviously something that is reviewed from time to time.

agency: Department of Health, Disability and Ageing
text: The definition of male and female, of sex, is reviewed?

agency: Department of Health, Disability and Ageing
text: No, no—the terminology that you're using, which is used by medical practitioners. I think we're talking about two different things. But the chief medical officer can probably answer that for you.

agency: Department of Health, Disability and Ageing
text: Sure. Just on the issue of gender incongruence, this is a term that's included, as you're mentioning, in the World Health Organization's International Classification of Diseases. So it's a very well-established term. It's not new terminology—
witness_organisation: Department of Health, Disability and Ageing
witness_position: Chief Medical Officer

agency: Department of Health, Disability and Ageing
text: Excuse me; why does something used by the World Health Organization make it well established?

agency: Department of Health, Disability and Ageing
text: Because it's used all over the world.
witness_organisation: Department of Health, Disability and Ageing
witness_position: Chief Medical Officer

agency: Department of Health, Disability and Ageing
text: Instead of gender dysphoria?

agency: Department of Health, Disability and Ageing
text: Gender dysphoria is used as well. Gender incongruence is—I can read the definitions, if you like, or I can share them with you out of session.
witness_organisation: Department of Health, Disability and Ageing
witness_position: Chief Medical Officer

agency: Department of Health, Disability and Ageing
text: Reading them is fine.

agency: Department of Health, Disability and Ageing
text: Gender incongruence is 'an objective difference or misalignment between your internal sense of gender and your biological sex assigned at birth'. Gender dysphoria is 'the psychological distress, discomfort or anxiety that can result from gender incongruence…not everyone with gender incongruence experiences severe distress and dysphoria is not an inherent requirement to identify as transgender'.
witness_organisation: Department of Health, Disability and Ageing
witness_position: Chief Medical Officer

agency: Department of Health, Disability and Ageing
text: So, Minister, can sex be changed by surgery?

agency: Department of Health, Disability and Ageing
text: Senator, the definitions that we're talking about—sex is what someone is. That's their characteristic at birth. Then we talk about gender in a few different ways, and that's not necessarily dependent on whether someone does or doesn't have surgery. I'd probably point you—we're getting outside the realm of the health department's responsibilities here—to state and territory based laws that look at certain characteristics that people have when deciding whether to issue a new birth certificate, for example. Then, of course, the Sex Discrimination Act recognises a range of people's attributes.

agency: Department of Health, Disability and Ageing
text: Attributes as opposed to sex at birth, which is chromosome—

agency: Department of Health, Disability and Ageing
text: It recognises gender and the attributes that relate to those genders.

agency: Department of Health, Disability and Ageing
text: So because it's in the law, it's right?

agency: Department of Health, Disability and Ageing
text: It's a law that's been in place for quite some time, Senator.

agency: Department of Health, Disability and Ageing
text: Since 2011, I think, with Julia Gillard.

agency: Department of Health, Disability and Ageing
text: Supported by the opposition at the time as well—yes.

agency: Department of Health, Disability and Ageing
text: And they're ruing the day. Decisions to add an item to Medicare are made using a legislative instrument in this case. Can you confirm the decision will be dealt with by way of a disallowable instrument?

agency: Department of Health, Disability and Ageing
text: That's a question for the department. I'm not sure what that legislative instrument usually would be.

We're sitting here today. The bill got discharged from the Notice Paper. The government then chose to immediately reintroduce that bill into the lower house, and that's where it is at the moment.

It's now close on six months since this was announced. There's been great concern expressed about the lack of information about the impact on the public hospital system. We've had just about all states and territories come out and be concerned about this. We're sitting here on 28 October, and I am seeking to understand what the broader implications on the public hospital system are. In the six months since this was announced it appears you have done no more work to try and determine what they are.

The only thing I have is a document that says 153,241 additional patient days are likely to occur in 2028-29 based on the evidence of the average cost of a stay in hospital. That's around $420 million a year. agency: Department of Health, Disability and Ageing
text: I'm interested in the budget measures regarding cheaper medicines. There have been several stages to this government's actions to make medicines cheaper that I want to understand. In July 2022, the government lowered the PBS safety net threshold. Can you tell me how that threshold works.

agency: Department of Health, Disability and Ageing
text: The PBS safety net places an upper limit on the co-payments that a patient may pay over the course of a calendar year. For general patients, who pay, at the moment, a $25 co-payment, once they reach the safety net, their co-payment is reduced to the concessional rate. For concessional patients, who currently pay $7.70 for each co-payment, once they reach the safety net for concessional patients, they no longer pay a co-payment at all, so the co-payment drops to zero. And there are thresholds that are separate for concessional and general patients.

It's a significant cost if you add that up times 52.

agency: Department of Health, Disability and Ageing
text:
Yes. The component I won't be able to answer is around the changes to Support at Home specifically. Under the Dose Administration Aids Program under the 8CPA—which as you know, is designed to assist patients living at home in the community to better manage their medicines with the objective of avoiding misadventures and improving medication adherence—the pharmacists identify eligible patients who live at home in the community, hold a Medicare or DVA card and a current government issued concession card, and either are having difficulty managing medicines due to literacy or language issues, physical disability or cognitive difficulties or take five or more prescription medicines and have difficulty managing them.

Where it intersects with the people receiving Support at Home services through aged-care funding is, if they are living at home in a community setting, they would meet the living situation eligibility for a government funded dose administration aid service provided by a participating pharmacy. Under the 8CPA—which, again, commenced on 1 July 2024—the weekly base caps for funded DAA services increased from 60 to 90 services per pharmacy for the duration of the 8CPA. It was an additional commitment of $196.7 million over the five years of the 8CPA to support that expanded DAA cap.

The DAA services funded under the program are not available—this may be something you already know, so apologies if you do—to inpatients of public or private hospitals, day hospital facilities or transitional care facilities; residents of residential aged-care homes; or patients in a correctional facility.

We have seen an increase in those services. If we look at 2024-25 compared to 2025-26, we've seen an increase in take-up. In 2025-26, we had more than 19.3 million DAA services that were delivered and funded. That was an increase of 700,000 services from 2024-25. Acknowledging your point, there is a funding limit at the pharmacy level, rather than a limit on whether an individual patient is eligible for a DAA service. We acknowledge that. We have seen in the most recent figures that, from around April 2026, approximately seven per cent of pharmacies reach that weekly cap.

text:
The bill that was reintroduced is the government policy. I can talk to you about the parliamentary processes. Essentially, if the government were to remove amendments or consider amendments, there are times where we would seek to provide supplementary explanatory memorandums, which we do quite often, or, of course, provide information during a committee debate in the Senate. agency: Department of Health, Disability and Ageing
text: No—

agency: Department of Health, Disability and Ageing

agency: Department of Health, Disability and Ageing
text: I have questions in relation to the Medicare assignment of benefits. I'm trying to get an idea. Could you perhaps provide an overview of the process that led to the decision to remove the verbal consent for AOB.

agency: Department of Health, Disability and Ageing
text: Firstly, it would be best to suggest that we haven't removed the process of verbal assignment of benefit. At the moment there is a transition period to the arrangements that the government has outlined for assignment of benefits, and the arrangements that have been in place for some time are still applying. The government's gone through a process of seeking to simplify the assignment of benefit process, and a broader range of options are now available to clinicians than was the case before those reforms, but it has also revealed the need for substantial education to assist clinicians to ensure that they can meet their assignment of benefit obligations and for the software industry to put in place structures that will make it easier for clinicians to do that. So, until such time as that's the case, there is an option which allows those who are having a benefit assigned to make some note that allows them to demonstrate that they did receive an assignment of benefit. That's what you're referring to by saying verbal assignment of benefit.
witness_organisation: Department of Health, Disability and Ageing
witness_position: First Assistant Secretary, Medicare Benefits and Digital Health Division

agency: Department of Health, Disability and Ageing
text: Basically, there was a decision that verbal assignment of benefit was going to be removed. There was, subsequently, quite a significant backlash, and my understanding is that there's been a 12-month deferral. Is that what you're referring to when you're saying that currently there still is a process by which verbal AOB is able to occur?

agency: Department of Health, Disability and Ageing
text: I'll ask Ms Riley to outline some further detail, but it has been continuously the case that clinicians are obliged to ensure that they can demonstrate that their benefit has been assigned. There are a range of ways that that can be done, and we are making that much easier for clinicians going forward.
witness_organisation: Department of Health, Disability and Ageing
witness_position: First Assistant Secretary, Medicare Benefits and Digital Health Division

agency: Department of Health, Disability and Ageing
text: Is it the view of the department that a requirement to seek AOB approval for every consult, such as in a setting like an aged-care home, is a feasible requirement, or is that one of the things that you may not pursue?

agency: Department of Health, Disability and Ageing
text: We've put in place provisions that ensure that there are viable options in a very broad range of circumstances. You're alluding to one where it can be more difficult to ensure that you have assignment of benefit. In some care settings, it can be difficult to get the consent of the person who's being treated, but there are ways that the legislation outlines that allow those people to assign their benefit, even in circumstances where they may not be able to do that themselves.
witness_organisation: Department of Health, Disability and Ageing
witness_position: First Assistant Secretary, Medicare Benefits and Digital Health Division

agency: Department of Health, Disability and Ageing
text: As part of that answer you've just given me, is the department looking to establish a mechanism to enable patients to assign an enduring assignment of benefit to reduce administrative burden?

agency: Department of Health, Disability and Ageing
text: Yes. There are already provisions in place that allow some categories of patients to do that. As we move into the final stage of this, there'll be further opportunities for people to have an enduring assignment of benefit. For patients that go to the same practice every time, there will be ways that they can provide an enduring assignment of benefit so they don't have to do that every time they visit that practice.
witness_organisation: Department of Health, Disability and Ageing
witness_position: First Assistant Secretary, Medicare Benefits and Digital Health Division

agency: Department of Health, Disability and Ageing
text: Can we be confident that the department will make sure that any changes that are going to be made long term will be effectively managed in a way to avoid a repeat of what happened this year, where the proposals were put out there at the very last minute? There was a very immediate backlash. We've, thankfully, had the 12-month reprieve to enable more work to be done. Are you confident that the processes that are now in place will avoid a repeat of what happened this year in relation to these changes to assignment of benefit?

agency: Department of Health, Disability and Ageing
text: The department takes very seriously the views of stakeholders when it is implementing policy. When it became clear to us that stakeholders wanted to have further discussions about how they could ensure they could comply with the law, we modified plans in sympathy with the issues they raised. What I can have confidence in is that, if there are further issues raised, we will listen to our stakeholders and we will seek to address those faithfully. But we have addressed those issues that have been raised to date, so, if the issues that have been raised to date are the only ones that come forward, then I can be confident that we will come through to implementation in the timeframes that have already been set out.
witness_organisation: Department of Health, Disability and Ageing
witness_position: First Assistant Secretary, Medicare Benefits and Digital Health Division

agency: Department of Health, Disability and Ageing
text: I look forward to seeing that. Can I just ask quickly—is Gardasil, the cervical cancer vaccine, in this one? It's the next one? Okay; cancel that. My understanding is that there was guidance sent to the private health insurers about how to treat the rebate changes that were being proposed by the bill, which has been subsequently discharged; is that correct?

agency: Department of Health, Disability and Ageing

witness_position: Deputy Secretary, Systems Strategy Group

agency: Department of Health, Disability and Ageing

witness_organisation: Department of Health, Disability and Ageing
witness_position: Deputy Secretary, Systems Strategy Group

agency: Department of Health, Disability and Ageing

The statement of expectation actually outlines what to do in acknowledging the parliament uncertainties—that's probably not the right word. It's about not making an assumption either way in terms of passage. The premium round has an explicit process for managing that. It has in the statement of expectations that, should there be amendments to the bill or any of those things, there'll be another opportunity to provide information into that premium round into that application process.
witness_organisation: Department of Health, Disability and Ageing
witness_position: Deputy Secretary, Systems Strategy Group

agency: Department of Health, Disability and Ageing
text: I understand there's a very significant process that precedes the announcement of the premium round changes. agency: Department of Health, Disability and Ageing
text: We would normally try and make sure we've got a decision by the end of January for the implementation from 1 April.
witness_organisation: Department of Health, Disability and Ageing
witness_position: Deputy Secretary, Systems Strategy Group

agency: Department of Health, Disability and Ageing
text: What do you want by the end of January?

agency: Department of Health, Disability and Ageing

witness_organisation: Department of Health, Disability and Ageing
witness_position: Deputy Secretary, Systems Strategy Group

agency: Department of Health, Disability and Ageing
text: How far before that would the sector need to know what the changes are likely to be? Obviously, they have to provide you with information. You have to provide back to them the response to that information. I understand there's a bit of a to-and-fro process to try and get to the lowest possible premium. When is that drop dead date?

agency: Department of Health, Disability and Ageing
text: What I'd just say with the statement of expectations—and then I'll pass it to Mr Hawkins—is that, in that, we acknowledge that there might not be that certainty prior to the applications, which is by 11 November. So I'm saying that we don't need to have made any updates to the insurers by that date. It would be beyond that date. I will pass to Mr Hawkins, but it was clearly articulated to insurers that, should there be any amendments or changes, we would have a subsequent process, and we would do that iteration. But I'll pass to Mr Hawkins.
witness_organisation: Department of Health, Disability and Ageing
witness_position: Deputy Secretary, Systems Strategy Group

agency: Department of Health, Disability and Ageing
text: Before you go to Mr Hawkins, I think my question wasn't so much around your promise to provide that consultative process. It was: when is the last possible time that the changes can come into effect to enable you to be able to go through the process that, obviously, you want to go through, you promised and need to go through with the sector in order for you to meet the 1 April deadline? All I want to know is just the date.

agency: Department of Health, Disability and Ageing
text: Yes. It would be difficult for me to give you an exact date—
witness_organisation: Department of Health, Disability and Ageing
witness_position: First Assistant Secretary, Portfolio Strategy Division

agency: Department of Health, Disability and Ageing
text: Fine. That's a good enough answer.

agency: Department of Health, Disability and Ageing
text: predominantly because, as you highlighted, often there can be significant to and fro. We did a bit of a change to the process last year and found that we could largely deal quite quickly with a number of insurers that worked with us and got their claims in. You can kind of whittle it down. There were two or three insurers that we had to have an iterative process with. But we're very conscious of that 1 April deadline and working with insurers through that process, and they're pretty agile at working with us when we give them feedback around the compliance or any issues that assist with their kinds of claims.
witness_organisation: Department of Health, Disability and Ageing
witness_position: First Assistant Secretary, Portfolio Strategy Division

agency: Department of Health, Disability and Ageing

agency: Department of Health, Disability and Ageing
text: The only thing I'd say here is that I think the characterisation of to and fro is a little bit different than if you have a binary choice of whether you're going to have a treatment or not, because that's a relatively easy thing to adjust in terms of what the premium offer is. It's kind of on or off.
witness_organisation: Department of Health, Disability and Ageing
witness_position: Secretary

agency: Department of Health, Disability and Ageing

agency: Department of Health, Disability and Ageing
text: Sure. There's only one more House/Senate sitting week.

agency: Department of Health, Disability and Ageing
text: Yes. That's what I'm talking about. I haven't seen the sitting calendar for next year. Maybe, Senator, you know what it is.

agency: Department of Health, Disability and Ageing
text: I was getting confused, because I thought that maybe there's only one week, and we don't have to come back so soon.

agency: Department of Health, Disability and Ageing
text: You'd know better than me if that were the case!

agency: Department of Health, Disability and Ageing

agency: Department of Health, Disability and Ageing

If that is not able to be met in terms of the changes, would it be fair to say that the changes could not occur for 1 April, given that we're not going to sit until February, unless Senator Green's going to tell me something really special.

agency: Department of Health, Disability and Ageing

witness_organisation: Department of Health, Disability and Ageing
witness_position: Secretary

agency: Department of Health, Disability and Ageing
text: So your answer is that it wouldn't rule it out. You could go as late as making a decision in February in order to still make the deadline.

agency: Department of Health, Disability and Ageing
text: Senator Ruston, I know we have a difference of opinion on this policy, but, just to make it clear, the government's committed to the policy, and we'd like to see it passed before the end of the year.

agency: Department of Health, Disability and Ageing
text: I'm sure you would. Finally, in the July and March PBAC meetings, the PBAC recommended a number of medicines be listed but only if the asking price were reduced. I'm just wondering if this is an increasing trend for PBAC to say they would recommend but only with a decreased price.

agency: Department of Health, Disability and Ageing
text: PBAC is committed to trying to keep as efficient as possible our recommendations as we deliberate, and with the utilisation of the pathways that we have for positive recommendations. We're trying to utilise those pathways as best as possible to give many opportunities to the sponsors with our advice and guidance as to how to progress to a successful listing.
witness_organisation: National Health and Medical Research Council
witness_position: Deputy Chair

agency: Department of Health, Disability and Ageing
text: Does PBAC advise companies on how much, specifically, they would need to reduce their price to be considered cost-effective in your analysis?

agency: Department of Health, Disability and Ageing
text: In our deliberations we're very conscious of setting out through our minutes, which are available to the sponsors at the end of the meeting, the ways to progress to a successful listing. That includes the economics, the clinical arrangements, and the way that we want them to see we would be able to establish a cost-effective price that would enable them to go forward.
witness_organisation: National Health and Medical Research Council
witness_position: Deputy Chair

agency: Department of Health, Disability and Ageing
text: That's great. Do you actually provide the sponsor with the specific analysis that you've made in your cost-effective analysis as part of your process, to say, 'We believe that, all things considered, your medicine is cost-effective at x price'?

agency: Department of Health, Disability and Ageing
text: Very specifically, yes.
witness_organisation: National Health and Medical Research Council
witness_position: Deputy Chair

agency: Department of Health, Disability and Ageing
text: How does PBAC determine when a price reduction on the applicant's price is required, and by how much? And how much of a consideration is that in the broader scheme of your considerations of an application for listing?

agency: Department of Health, Disability and Ageing
text: It's a critical aspect of the application's evaluation and assessment. It goes through a range of technical assessment before it even reaches PBAC, not only with the independent and external academic evaluation process but also through our subcommittees—the drug utilisation subcommittee and the economics subcommittee. PBAC's deliberation, after all that breadth of work and the scope of the submission being analysed, is looking at a price claimed by a sponsor that it wants for its product. PBAC considers looking at incremental, comparative cost-effectiveness measurements whether or not that incremental benefit—compared to the standard therapy, alternative therapy or standard of care—both at a clinical level and at a value or economic level, is going to be worth so much. If that doesn't meet what the sponsor has proposed as its claimed price then we try to give guidance as to what would meet that.
witness_organisation: National Health and Medical Research Council
witness_position: Deputy Chair

agency: Department of Health, Disability and Ageing
text: As a specific example, there has been quite a bit of commentary in relation to multiple sclerosis drugs. I'm sure you're aware of it. I don't need to go through the whole preamble—you know what I'm talking about, don't you?

agency: Department of Health, Disability and Ageing
text: I do.
witness_organisation: National Health and Medical Research Council
witness_position: Deputy Chair

text: When did PBAC originally recommend that these new medicines—Ocrevus and Kesimta—be listed on the PBS?

agency: Department of Health, Disability and Ageing
text: Sorry, I don't go by the brand names. At PBAC we use the—
witness_organisation: National Health and Medical Research Council
witness_position: Deputy Chair

agency: Department of Health, Disability and Ageing
text: You're going to try to make me pronounce them, aren't you?

agency: Department of Health, Disability and Ageing
text: I am, and I'll enjoy watching it.
witness_organisation: National Health and Medical Research Council
witness_position: Deputy Chair

agency: Department of Health, Disability and Ageing
text: That was one thing Greg Hunt was incredibly good at! I'm not even going to try. We're talking about the multiple sclerosis medicines that went before PBAC. When did PBAC originally recommend these medicines be listed on the PBS?

agency: Department of Health, Disability and Ageing
text: I'll have to go back and look. There are quite a number of medicines for MS. In regard to the issue that led to the PBAC recommending a review of all the relapsing remitting multiple sclerosis medicines that is currently underway, we listed a new medicine. In that recommendation going forward, pricing policy came into effect as part of the negotiations between the department and the sponsor. I would just remind everyone there is a delineation between the role of the PBAC and the role of the department.
witness_organisation: National Health and Medical Research Council
witness_position: Deputy Chair

agency: Department of Health, Disability and Ageing
text: My understanding is the department referred this matter as it directly related to the delisting of these medicines. Do I understand correctly that, at the time of the original decision, the PBAC determined that these medicines were more effective than the older treatment? We're delisting the older treatments, and the new medicines were more effective than the older treatments—is that fair?—hence the higher price was acceptable.

agency: Department of Health, Disability and Ageing
text: No, I don't think that's a totally accurate way I would describe the deliberations for the latest the newest medicine, which that was given a positive recommendation. The basis of the positive recommendation of the latest medicine for multiple sclerosis was as a cost-minimisation recommendation, with all that goes with it. With the current pricing policies and the application of reference pricing, what it does is give effect then for the pricing area of the department to look at the flow-on effects, if you like, to what is basically price reductions.
witness_organisation: National Health and Medical Research Council
witness_position: Deputy Chair

agency: Department of Health, Disability and Ageing
text: I note that the minister's made public comments at press conferences that he'd like to see these drugs remain on the PBS. Would PBAC consider those public comments by the minister to be an instruction under the National Health Act from the decision-maker or just a standard input like any other consumer or MS patient? Does the minister's commentary have hold greater weight or sway as it relates to the National Health Act?

agency: Department of Health, Disability and Ageing
text: No, it doesn't.
witness_organisation: National Health and Medical Research Council
witness_position: Deputy Chair

agency: Department of Health, Disability and Ageing
text: When is PBAC likely to make the determination in relation to the ongoing listings?

agency: Department of Health, Disability and Ageing
text: We have what we call a rapid review under way. It's being carried out by the department with advice from our previous consideration to the department about that review and the scope of it. Part of the work is being undertaken also by an external academic group. We've got the department working with that external academic group. We've held one stakeholder meeting with our expert clinicians and the MS Australia patient networks. We have asked the department to bring the report back to us for the December intracycle meeting of PBAC, at which point we'll be looking at what's there and having a discussion about where it all sits.
witness_organisation: National Health and Medical Research Council
witness_position: Deputy Chair

agency: Department of Health, Disability and Ageing
text: What has been your involvement or PBAC's involvement—I understand you're only acting as the chair at the moment—in the work of the process of the HTA review?

agency: Department of Health, Disability and Ageing
text: As you've already heard tonight, we've had briefings from relevant departmental officers as chair and deputy chair. We've had those briefings under probity and protected access. They've been briefings partly as a courtesy and partly as statutory officeholders hoping to also be able to provide input or advice to the department officers as they see fit.
witness_organisation: National Health and Medical Research Council
witness_position: Deputy Chair

agency: Department of Health, Disability and Ageing
text: You've seen the final report of the HTA review of the implementation advisory group?

agency: Department of Health, Disability and Ageing
text: In December 2025, the HTA chairs forum, which is all of the HTA chairs across the office of HTA, were given a briefing by the then chair of the implementation advisory group in confidence and as a courtesy.
witness_organisation: National Health and Medical Research Council
witness_position: Deputy Chair

agency: Department of Health, Disability and Ageing

witness_organisation: National Health and Medical Research Council
witness_position: Deputy Chair
