text: That brings us to the end of this outcome. Rather than do a short round of the next outcome and get new officials to the table, the committee will take a short suspension, and we will reconvene for outcome 1.

agency: Department of Health, Disability and Ageing
text: We recommence with outcome 1, health policy access and support and cross-portfolio Indigenous matters. We're joined again by Senator the Hon. Jennie McAllister, Minister for the National Disability Insurance Scheme, representing the Minister for Health, Disability and Ageing. For the benefit of new senators in the room, we had listed the Centre for Disease Control and the National Rural Health Commission for this evening. We've let them go home because we don't believe we'll get to them tonight. They'll be here tomorrow if you do have questions for them. I call officers from the Department of Health, Disability and Ageing in relation to outcome 1, and I will perhaps go to Senator Ruston for the first round of questions.

agency: Department of Health, Disability and Ageing
text: I'd like to ask some questions about the prostate cancer nurses. Could people who can answer the questions in relation to the Gardasil rates be ready to go next. What was the rationale behind the decision to redirect funding for specialist prostate cancer nurse funding from PCFA to the McGrath Foundation?

agency: Department of Health, Disability and Ageing
text: We probably need to start with the Australian Cancer Plan, which really presented a vision for a far more coordinated, nationally consistent approach to both navigation and support and a strengthened workforce. It was really trying to reflect a vision of more people accessing support from a Commonwealth funded nurse. They were also seeking to get more consistent support across cancers and geographic area for a national model of care for this sort of cancer support. It also talks about streamlined approaches for health services in terms of, in the previous models, a range of different types of organisations funding health services for different types of cancer nurses. I think the seed was set with the Australian Cancer Plan. In late 2023, the government signalled to the organisations that were providing cancer nurses of the intention of this more coordinated approach.
witness_organisation: Department of Health, Disability and Ageing
witness_position: Deputy Secretary, Prevention, Primary Care and Medicare Group

agency: Department of Health, Disability and Ageing
text: Were there any concerns about the way PCFA was running the program?

agency: Department of Health, Disability and Ageing
text: Not to my knowledge, no.
witness_organisation: Department of Health, Disability and Ageing
witness_position: Deputy Secretary, Prevention, Primary Care and Medicare Group

agency: Department of Health, Disability and Ageing
text: The decision was purely around the streamlining of a service as opposed to there being any concerns. I'm interested. PCFA was awarded their grant in 2024. Has anything changed since that time when they were awarded the grant that would have been a catalyst for them no longer providing this service to the people they represent?

agency: Department of Health, Disability and Ageing
text: This change to the model was signalled to the sector, as I said, in late 2023. We have seen the transition of melanoma nurses and lung cancer nurses, and the prostate ones are the next ones to join the model.
witness_organisation: Department of Health, Disability and Ageing
witness_position: Deputy Secretary, Prevention, Primary Care and Medicare Group

agency: Department of Health, Disability and Ageing
text: When was PCFA formally notified of the decision?

agency: Department of Health, Disability and Ageing
text: There were discussions in late 2023. Their funding had been extended for a short time, and that does expire in the middle of next year. In terms of the confirmation of the expiration of that planned funding at the end of June 2027, I think it was myself and Professor Dorothy Keefe from Cancer Australia that spoke to the Chair and the CEO of PCFA in late August this year.
witness_organisation: Department of Health, Disability and Ageing
witness_position: Deputy Secretary, Prevention, Primary Care and Medicare Group

agency: Department of Health, Disability and Ageing
text: You're saying that in 2023 PCFA were notified of the intention of this change to come about. Is that correct?

agency: Department of Health, Disability and Ageing
text: There were discussions with a range of sector organisations about the government's intention to move to this model. At that time, I understand that the PCFA expressed their concerns about that. Subsequently, their funding was extended to the point where it is now.
witness_organisation: Department of Health, Disability and Ageing
witness_position: Deputy Secretary, Prevention, Primary Care and Medicare Group

agency: Department of Health, Disability and Ageing
text: Okay. Back to the original question: when was PCFA notified formally of the decision not to continue their funding after the extension and for the nurses to move into a different—

witness_organisation: Department of Health, Disability and Ageing
witness_position: Deputy Secretary, Prevention, Primary Care and Medicare Group

agency: Department of Health, Disability and Ageing

witness_position: Deputy Secretary, Prevention, Primary Care and Medicare Group

witness_organisation: Department of Health, Disability and Ageing
witness_position: Deputy Secretary, Prevention, Primary Care and Medicare Group

agency: Department of Health, Disability and Ageing

text: I've got a question in relation to a question on notice from the last estimates, SQ26-002938. In your answer to my question it says that the government has invested $610 million in suicide prevention since 2022-23. The Auditor-General found that government objectives to reduce suicide had not been achieved. The Productivity Commission found no change in suicide rates since the national agreement was signed. What has the $610 million bought?

agency: Department of Health, Disability and Ageing
text:
Obviously, that funding figure is over a multi-year period. We probably directly invest in the order of about $130 million a year into suicide prevention. This delivers a range of things. So there is a range of funding that sits under the National Mental Health and Suicide Prevention Agreement that provides a range of funding for what we call aftercare, which are services for people that had have made a suicide attempt, and it helps them from there. It's very evidence based in terms of providing support. If you can provide those supports into that period from when they're hospitalised or whatever, then you tend to get fewer repeat attempts and those types of behaviours coming through. So it's quite evidence based for that. We also fund a postvention support service, which is basically for people bereaved from suicide. That's run by Youturn Australia and provides a range of services for immediate family members and loved ones that are bereaved from suicide because there are, of course, risks and obviously they have significant needs through that episode.

From there then we run also what we were discussing before, the National Suicide Prevention Leadership and Support Program. That provides a range of services to people, and it funds some programs, like MATES in Construction, which I think we discussed last time we were here. It funds a range of programs and some First Nations programs. It also funds some leadership and provides some research funding for some organisations to go and provide broader leadership for the suicide sector. It also funds some communications and also some supports for priority populations. So it provides actually quite a diverse range of programs and supports for people from a range of different fronts.

I would also add that that's probably just the direct suicide programs that we have. They are also supplemented by our crisis lines and things like Lifeline et cetera that we provide that are not included in that funding. They have quite sustained high usage for people in distress and a range of other things as well. Outside of that funding, we also have things like our Medicare mental health clinics, which work with distressed individuals and suicidality as well when people go into there. So we actually have quite a range of services. Obviously the data remain fairly static over a long period of time.

There isn't necessarily a direct causality between those programs and the national suicide rate at that level. Some of the programs might be small-ish programs on their own, and so getting a direct attribution of that to the broader suicide rate is very difficult. But all of them have indicators or metrics regarding what those programs have achieved and done. I think we put a range of that information towards a previous question on notice that we answered, which we'd be happy to redo, if that's of use.
witness_organisation: Department of Health, Disability and Ageing
witness_position: First Assistant Secretary, Mental Health and Suicide Prevention Division

agency: Department of Health, Disability and Ageing
text: For all the money we're spending, I don't think we are moving the dial, are we? The headline number of people that are taking their own lives doesn't seem to be changing.

agency: Department of Health, Disability and Ageing
text: At a headline level, yes. Obviously, the general rate of suicide has been relatively stable for a reasonably long period of time. It moves around a little bit but not significantly. The usage of many of the services we've got remains quite significant and growing. You don't know the counterfactual—I think the perception would be this: if we weren't running those programs, would anything be any different? Quite possibly it would be significantly higher. We don't know that, but there would definitely be a risk of that. So I think it's probably a little bit simplistic to say that, because the rate has changed, those programs are not making any difference.
witness_organisation: Department of Health, Disability and Ageing
witness_position: First Assistant Secretary, Mental Health and Suicide Prevention Division

agency: Department of Health, Disability and Ageing
text: I'm not suggesting they're not making a difference, but the numbers are still too high. By the time we come back tomorrow morning from today, seven men will have taken their lives. I think that's a national crisis that we should be doing something about. We're spending money, but it's still too many. The National Suicide Prevention Strategy was launched in February 2025. The Auditor-General reported that, as of 25 September, there was no implementation plan, and the advisory group had not even been set up. The Auditor-General recommended you write a plan, and the department agreed only in principle. Is there an implementation plan today?

agency: Department of Health, Disability and Ageing
text:
As just a little bit of context for that—we want to be careful with that—that audit was about the department, not the broader policy decision-making of government in that audit. So, in terms of the plan, I think, when the department agreed in part, that was largely because it is not of the department's own making such that it can agree to a full implementation plan that would cut across pretty much all portfolios across government or indeed state and territory governments. That strategy is very much a whole-of-nation strategy and has actions for pretty much all Commonwealth portfolios and states and territories as well. So it is not within the department's remit to do an implementation plan that would be agreed to by all those jurisdictions. That is a matter ultimately for government—and governments—to consider. That was the basis for agreeing to that recommendation and putting those caveats on it.

The development of an implementation plan is something that I think we have discussed in a couple of committees, probably not with yourself. There is a range of work that the National Suicide Prevention Office is doing around its outcomes framework that we think has some necessary pieces of work that will help us inform that. They are also doing a piece of work to look at, effectively, a baseline of what is happening against the actions in the strategy at the moment and to start to recommend where they think the areas of focus are. That will basically inform, I think, where government goes on that journey.
witness_organisation: Department of Health, Disability and Ageing
witness_position: First Assistant Secretary, Mental Health and Suicide Prevention Division

agency: Department of Health, Disability and Ageing
text: So is there an implementation plan?

agency: Department of Health, Disability and Ageing

There are a range of things that government is doing that are informed by those broader strategies, because the strategy also cuts across a lot of the other economic and social indicators that the government considers when it takes action more broadly, which is the point of doing a stocktake and getting a baseline from the National Suicide Prevention Office, who are here today as well, if you have any questions for them.

There is a requirement for two, obviously for the importance of the woman and baby's safety and to manage elements such as fatigue. So there is a requirement for two—and, in most cases, it is two midwives who attend the birth at home in support of that woman. text: My understanding of the scenario for many home births, particularly in regional and rural Australia, is that, firstly, as you said, you need at least two medical practitioners present. What are you going to do if you're a privately practising midwife asked to attend a home birth in regional and rural Australia and the person you normally call on to accompany you to this home birth is a second, is not endorsed and can't get insurance. What happens then?

agency: Department of Health, Disability and Ageing
text: This was quite a significant change when the insurance product became available. In preparation for an insurance product and the sunsetting of the exemption, an 18-month grace period was allowed for in order to allow sufficient time for those that were intending to attend home births to become eligible for the insurance. In addition, there was an investment in scholarships that midwives were entitled to make an application for that would support them in the additional study required in order to complete the eligibility to become an endorsed midwife. We put a number of mechanisms in place in preparation for the change from the removal of the exemption on 31 December this year.

witness_position: First Assistant Secretary, Chief Nurse, Health Professions Advisory Division

agency: Department of Health, Disability and Ageing
text: But to become endorsed, as I understand it, you need at least 5,000 hours or the equivalent of three years of full-time clinical practice. How are you going to do that in 18 months?

agency: Department of Health, Disability and Ageing
text: You don't have to do it in 18 months to be able to demonstrate those 5,000 hours of experience.
witness_organisation: Department of Health, Disability and Ageing
witness_position: First Assistant Secretary, Chief Nurse, Health Professions Advisory Division

agency: Department of Health, Disability and Ageing
text: But, if you were a second midwife and you were told the exemption is running out in 18 months, you'd think, 'I'd better get endorsed,' but you've only got 18 months of runway and you need to get 5,000 hours—three years of experience.

agency: Department of Health, Disability and Ageing
text: It is over six years that they need to have built up that number of hours. It doesn't need to be in the last 18 months. We weren't suggesting we were trying to make sure they had that number of hours within 18 months. They would have been able to bank some of those hours from previous service. For the safety of the birth, it's about making sure we have two qualified people that can support one another, and all medical practitioners do need to have indemnity insurance. The exemption was because there weren't products available. The products are available. It is important that we make sure that we're providing a safe service.

text: I have two points on that. Firstly, I take your point about it being within the past six years, but from what I understand a lot of these people are commencing a career as a midwife. I don't understand. Was thought given to designing an insurance product that the Commonwealth was underwriting that would ensure that seconds had some level of insurance coverage?

agency: Department of Health, Disability and Ageing
text: When the policy was considered, this had been an issue for a number of years. The view was that the insurance product be available to endorsed midwives. Endorsed midwives reflect a level of experience. You would want midwives attending a homebirth who had completed 5,000 hours of experience or were able to demonstrate that experience, because of the importance of identification of risk, early escalation and the safe care of mother and baby from a home may need identification and movement to a hospital. That experienced midwife at homebirth was considered an important part of the policy. Endorsed midwives are experienced midwives because of the requirement of the 5,000 hours before they're eligible to be endorsed. With that comes the ability to prescribe and to order tests as well.
witness_organisation: Department of Health, Disability and Ageing
witness_position: First Assistant Secretary, Chief Nurse, Health Professions Advisory Division

agency: Department of Health, Disability and Ageing
text: I understand the explanation you're giving. I don't accept the rationale. My concern is that we have a situation where an endorsed midwife that has a level of experience will always be attending the homebirth, but we have a situation now where the person they would normally take with them in regional and rural areas where a lot of these other health practitioners are not readily available and are not going to be available or have insurance. You're either taking someone who doesn't have insurance, potentially—I don't think you're doing that if you're an endorsed midwife—or if you're committed to having a homebirth you're possibly doing it without any medical assistance. Have those consequences been modelled and thought through? From what I understand from groups like Homebirth Australia and others, this is their concern.

agency: Department of Health, Disability and Ageing
text: That was a lot in one step. The Nurse and Midwifery Board of Australia are currently reviewing the requirements for an endorsed midwife. That review is underway, but it will not be complete before the end of this calendar year. We have been working and meeting on a regular basis with Homebirth Australia, as the chief midwife did today. We continue to work with them in order that we can encourage those making their birth choices around—if a second midwife is not available at birth, then other birthing choices are offered to the woman in a timely way. It is important to emphasise that birthing without a health professional with you is a very dangerous thing to do, and we would not encourage anyone to do that. We would encourage them to seek guidance through their midwife as to the best available option to them if home birth is no longer going to be a choice for them at that time. The other thing is that, in this time that we've been working on this, the growth in public funded home birth has increased significantly. Almost all states and territories are now delivering publicly funded home birth as well. The final state is Tasmania, and it is working towards publicly funded home birth as well.

witness_position: First Assistant Secretary, Chief Nurse, Health Professions Advisory Division

agency: Department of Health, Disability and Ageing
text: An investigation by the Age found that the TGA assessed applications for 55,223 medical devices in the last decade, so from 2016 to 2026. In that time only 4.3 per cent of applications were subject to a conformity assessment and only 830 devices were rejected. Is that an appropriate or representative percentage of devices to subject to conformity assessments?

agency: Department of Health, Disability and Ageing
text: I'll start answering the question and then hand over to my colleague Mr Jamieson. To understand the regulatory arrangements in Australia—we have two pathways for supplying in Australia. The first pathway is seeking a TGA conformity assessment, and the other pathway is where a manufacturer can use a conformity assessment certificate that's issued by another recognised regulator from overseas. But, in all cases, conformity assessment is a cornerstone of what the regulations require. Depending on the classification of the device, the elements in relation to conformity assessment then are commensurate with the risk of the device itself. In terms of the numbers that you quoted I think, Mr Jamieson, those numbers of four per cent are in relation to TGA conformity assessments.
witness_organisation: Department of Health, Disability and Ageing
witness_position: First Assistant Secretary, Medical Devices and Product Quality Division

agency: Department of Health, Disability and Ageing
text: Yes, those percentages are roughly correct, so that would be—
witness_organisation: Department of Health, Disability and Ageing
witness_position: Assistant Secretary, Medical Devices and Product Quality Division

agency: Department of Health, Disability and Ageing
text: It seems a bit low.

agency: Department of Health, Disability and Ageing
text: As my colleague Ms Duffy explained, that's only those manufacturers who need to come to the TGA for certification. It doesn't include the bulk of manufacturers who have had equivalent certification from another regulator.
witness_organisation: Department of Health, Disability and Ageing
witness_position: Assistant Secretary, Medical Devices and Product Quality Division

agency: Department of Health, Disability and Ageing
text: In other countries?

agency: Department of Health, Disability and Ageing
text:
Can I add a couple of elements of context as well. We are, like many other regulators, a risk based regulator. Our role is to fundamentally recognise that there are risks to balance in regulating therapeutic goods in Australia, regardless of whether they're medicines, devices, biologicals or others. That risk is frequently one between safety and quality and access. We can set the bar very high on safety and quality and ensure that Australians never have access to emerging or innovative devices or therapeutic goods. So our role is to ensure that the balance is set appropriately between access, and safety and quality. And we do that in a number of ways. As my colleagues have described, one of those is reliance on the decisions of overseas regulators. I'm not just saying that with abandon. It's actually having an understanding around the practices of those other regulators and using those as inputs into our decisions.

The only other thing I'd say is that it's important not to take those authorisation decisions in isolation, that our regulation of therapeutic goods occurs across the entire life cycle. So we're balancing the risk between the premarket authorisation decisions and the postmarket monitoring and vigilance mechanisms that we have in place for the life cycle of that product.
witness_organisation: Department of Health, Disability and Ageing
witness_position: Deputy Secretary, Health Products Regulation Group

agency: Department of Health, Disability and Ageing

agency: Department of Health, Disability and Ageing

agency: Department of Health, Disability and Ageing

In those circumstances, do you apply any stronger review process because there might be some concern about the independence of that assessment?

agency: Department of Health, Disability and Ageing
text: I'm assuming you're talking about notified bodies in Europe.
witness_organisation: Department of Health, Disability and Ageing
witness_position: First Assistant Secretary, Medical Devices and Product Quality Division

agency: Department of Health, Disability and Ageing

agency: Department of Health, Disability and Ageing
text: The genesis of the notified bodies in Europe is that they did actually start off as being government entities. And then, through processes and decisions made by the European Council, they were then privatised. Similar to how the TGA undertakes its work, it's fee for service. So notified bodies also operate under a fee-for-service model, just the same as TGA. Many regulators around the world are moving to fee for service as well. So the model is well established. In terms of conflicts and other aspects to this, that is something that is deeply looked at by the competent authorities in the countries where these notified bodies are established, and there is a very rigorous mechanism under which the notified bodies are assessed and reassessed by the competent authorities and an overarching group that looks at and assesses them on a groupwide perspective across Europe.
witness_organisation: Department of Health, Disability and Ageing
witness_position: First Assistant Secretary, Medical Devices and Product Quality Division

agency: Department of Health, Disability and Ageing
text: While we're talking about overseas medical devices, are all overseas warnings about device risks passed on by you to us consumers?

agency: Department of Health, Disability and Ageing
text: It does depend on the overseas warning and the actual device itself, whether or not it's supplied in Australia. My colleague Dr Noja may like to extrapolate on that a little bit.
witness_organisation: Department of Health, Disability and Ageing
witness_position: First Assistant Secretary, Medical Devices and Product Quality Division

agency: Department of Health, Disability and Ageing
text: It's a really important question to ask, what happens in the postmarket space. I think previously at this committee we've spoken about the various feeds that we have in respect to signals. We look at adverse events, we look at the emerging evidence, we speak to international regulators—and we do that monthly. In addition to that, we have regular information exchange with them that includes information directly through to the postmarket teams as well as to our recalls teams. Sometimes, when we look at actions that happen in other countries, we need to see whether those products are supplied in Australia. Additionally, sometimes things can occur in one particular country that don't necessarily occur in Australia because of the different population that we have. So we consider all of that, but, where appropriate, of course we will undertake market action if we feel so—
witness_organisation: Department of Health, Disability and Ageing
witness_position: Assistant Secretary, Medical Devices and Product Quality Division

agency: Department of Health, Disability and Ageing
text: So it's when the warning is just inapplicable in Australia that it's not passed on, but it otherwise is; is that right?

agency: Department of Health, Disability and Ageing
text: If we believe there is an impact on the Australian population, we will action—yes.
witness_organisation: Department of Health, Disability and Ageing
witness_position: Assistant Secretary, Medical Devices and Product Quality Division

agency: Department of Health, Disability and Ageing
text: Okay. Thank you. I think that's—

agency: Department of Health, Disability and Ageing
text: Just to complement that, there have been instances where there has been community interest because they have become aware of something that's happening overseas. We will post something on our website to clarify that, even though there might be a signal overseas, the product may not be available in Australia so that we're able to provide that information to the community to understand that they're in no danger here in Australia.
witness_organisation: Department of Health, Disability and Ageing
witness_position: First Assistant Secretary, Medical Devices and Product Quality Division

agency: Department of Health, Disability and Ageing

witness_organisation: Department of Health, Disability and Ageing

agency: Department of Health, Disability and Ageing

agency: Department of Health, Disability and Ageing

witness_organisation: Department of Health, Disability and Ageing

witness_position: First Assistant Secretary, Health Security and Immunisation Division

agency: Department of Health, Disability and Ageing

witness_organisation: Department of Health, Disability and Ageing

agency: Department of Health, Disability and Ageing

witness_organisation: Department of Health, Disability and Ageing

agency: Department of Health, Disability and Ageing

witness_organisation: Department of Health, Disability and Ageing

agency: Department of Health, Disability and Ageing
text: Okay. Sweden has just changed its vaccine schedule. In a procurement shift, they have removed mRNA COVID vaccines and replaced mRNA COVID shots with the old way of doing it: protein based vaccines—specifically, Nuvaxovid. For clarity, mRNA has not been banned—I'm not saying it's been banned—just removed from the schedule. Will you follow suit and drop mRNA vaccines? If not, what is Sweden getting wrong? Why do you disagree?

agency: Department of Health, Disability and Ageing
text: Just going back to your previous question, I've got more available information at hand. The vaccine that you're referring to in Australia is referred to as Novavax, and it is actually approved by the TGA but isn't available. The company made an independent decision not to continue manufacturing that vaccine that has regulatory approval, so we are unable to get stock of it. That's why it's not in Australia.
witness_organisation: Department of Health, Disability and Ageing
witness_position: First Assistant Secretary, Health Security and Immunisation Division

agency: Department of Health, Disability and Ageing
text: Thank you very much, Dr Peatt. Can you tell me why, if you know—I don't 100 per cent expect you to know—they are not selling it here?

agency: Department of Health, Disability and Ageing
text: That's an individual decision for that company.
witness_organisation: Department of Health, Disability and Ageing
witness_position: First Assistant Secretary, Health Security and Immunisation Division

agency: Department of Health, Disability and Ageing
text: So what's Sweden getting wrong—going back to my second question?

agency: Department of Health, Disability and Ageing
text: I'm happy to refer to Professor Gibney on the individual decisions and recommendations around what's contained in Australia's immunisation recommendations and schedule. But we've had the conversation previously around the fact that different decisions are made in different countries, and they're based on issues such as demography, epidemiology and the emerging disease patterns. We also are not in the position of questioning or making judgements about other countries' clinical decisions. I don't know, Professor Gibney, whether there's anything you'd like to add.
witness_organisation: Department of Health, Disability and Ageing
witness_position: Deputy Secretary, Health Products Regulation Group

agency: Department of Health, Disability and Ageing
text: There's no reason for us to comment on Sweden's decision about which vaccine they purchase. We're happy with the mRNA vaccine that we have available for COVID, and ATAGI don't have any plans to request another company to come in and try and provide an alternative vaccine. We have a vaccine available.
witness_organisation: Department of Health, Disability and Ageing
witness_position: Co-Chair, Australian Technical Advisory Group on Immunisation

agency: Department of Health, Disability and Ageing
text: With due respect, I think this issue is fairly serious. When a country that led the way in many ways on the correct response to COVID changes its mind, I would surely expect you to ask why and find out why.

agency: Department of Health, Disability and Ageing
text: We certainly review policy updates from other national immunisation technical advisory groups, and we routinely do that, but there are a whole range of reasons why a country might choose one vaccine over another, and that does not necessarily need to initiate a change in Australia. In this case, it would not initiate a change.
witness_organisation: Department of Health, Disability and Ageing
witness_position: Co-Chair, Australian Technical Advisory Group on Immunisation

agency: Department of Health, Disability and Ageing
text: I would have thought, in the interest of protecting the people of Australia, that if a country like Sweden changes its mind you would inquire why and say either, 'This is why we are not changing our mind,' or, 'This is why we are changing our mind.' Could you take that on notice, please, because I think the question deserves a better answer in writing.

agency: Department of Health, Disability and Ageing
text: Certainly. We can take that on notice.
witness_organisation: Department of Health, Disability and Ageing
witness_position: Co-Chair, Australian Technical Advisory Group on Immunisation

agency: Department of Health, Disability and Ageing
text: Thank you, Professor.

agency: Department of Health, Disability and Ageing
text: My colleague Mr Henderson, I know, has to say something, but I would just highlight that I know that there are different positions and views on some of the actions and public health measures that were undertaken during COVID, but I think it's fairly well recognised around the world that both our vaccination rates and the extent to which that vaccination led to a reduction in mortality and morbidity is such that I take your point that Sweden is an example to many countries; so is Australia's vaccine response an example to many countries in terms of a successful vaccine rollout and management of the challenges that COVID presented. So I'm not sure that we need to necessarily be looking to other countries as an example. The regulatory decisions that we take and the scientific approach that ATAGI provides and the National Immunisation Program all serve Australia well.
witness_organisation: Department of Health, Disability and Ageing
witness_position: Deputy Secretary, Health Products Regulation Group

agency: Department of Health, Disability and Ageing
text: If that's the case and you don't want to do it and Professor Gibney does it, that's fine, but surely you need to justify yourself with references because Sweden has the attention of many people around the world.

agency: Department of Health, Disability and Ageing
text: Yes, I think that that's probably true. But unless there's actually a specific—when you say 'with references', I think it's actually quite clear, and we've provided evidence previously around the success of the vaccine rollout in Australia and where we have performed in terms of mortality by population around the world. We performed very well. As we've highlighted previously, the risk-benefit profile at a population level of the vaccines that we both approved and recommended remains overwhelmingly positive. I'm not convinced that a case has been made as to why we should conform to the practices of another country.
witness_organisation: Department of Health, Disability and Ageing
witness_position: Deputy Secretary, Health Products Regulation Group

agency: Department of Health, Disability and Ageing
text: I'm not saying you should conform. I'm saying: why don't you check? Surely, if I were in your position, I'd be checking and saying, 'They've got it wrong; here's why,' or, 'They've got it right; we'll change.'

agency: Department of Health, Disability and Ageing
text: But, by that suggestion, I think what you're suggesting is that we should review the vaccination decisions of 190 other countries and work out that ours is the best. I think I've highlighted previously that we make our own sovereign decisions and that we undertake appropriate review on the regulatory decisions that we make. Professor Gibney and the other members of ATAGI provide their scientific expertise in those decisions, and they're solid decisions.
witness_organisation: Department of Health, Disability and Ageing
witness_position: Deputy Secretary, Health Products Regulation Group

agency: Department of Health, Disability and Ageing
text: Do I really need to remind you what your predecessor, Professor Skerritt, said to me when I asked him if they'd done testing on the COVID shots here? He said, 'No, Senator, we relied upon the FDA in America.' At that time, the FDA had previously announced that they did no testing and relied entirely on Pfizer, which killed—

agency: Department of Health, Disability and Ageing
text: If I may, I'm more than happy to have a conversation again around the process that we undertake and that reliance is not simply accepting the decisions of other regulators and that we have a very robust—
witness_organisation: Department of Health, Disability and Ageing
witness_position: Deputy Secretary, Health Products Regulation Group

agency: Department of Health, Disability and Ageing
text: So Professor Skerritt got it wrong?

agency: Department of Health, Disability and Ageing
text: I'm not going to comment on Professor Skerritt's discussions with you previously.
witness_organisation: Department of Health, Disability and Ageing
witness_position: Deputy Secretary, Health Products Regulation Group

agency: Department of Health, Disability and Ageing
text: That's what the whole basis of our vaccine rollout was.

agency: Department of Health, Disability and Ageing
text: Senator Roberts, please don't speak over the witnesses. They should be given the opportunity to answer your question.

agency: Department of Health, Disability and Ageing
text: Professor Lawler has talked about us not necessarily exhaustively looking at every country when they make a different decision on something, but it is true we engage very actively internationally with regulatory peers to understand trends in a whole range of things. In fact, Professor Lawler is chair of an international organisation of regulators so that we share information about the emerging trends. So I think I'd just put that in the context that we are not blind to what happens internationally. We can certainly potentially engage with our Swedish colleagues, but we do scan the international environment on a very regular basis.
witness_organisation: Department of Health, Disability and Ageing
witness_position: Secretary

agency: Department of Health, Disability and Ageing
text: Right, and that's all I'm asking for, on notice.

agency: Department of Health, Disability and Ageing
text: I just want to clarify that, in relation to Nuvaxovid, it's only the original strain that is registered, so it's not the most recent strains of COVID-19 that are on the ARTG.
witness_organisation: Department of Health, Disability and Ageing
witness_position: First Assistant Secretary, Medicines Regulation Division

agency: Department of Health, Disability and Ageing
text: Thank you; I appreciate it.

agency: Department of Health, Disability and Ageing
text: You have one final question, Senator Roberts, and then I'll have to rotate.

agency: Department of Health, Disability and Ageing
text: I've got two questions that go together.

agency: Department of Health, Disability and Ageing
text: If you can turn it into one question, that'd be great.

agency: Department of Health, Disability and Ageing
text: Are hydroxychloroquine and ivermectin available to doctors to prescribe for influenza and related illness? Are we now letting doctors use their training and professional judgement in the best interests of their patients again or not? Prior to the pandemic, both ivermectin and hydroxychloroquine were legally available for Australian doctors to prescribe without a knock on the door from AHPRA. For clarity, no other medication was ever recommended for influenza and similar illnesses. With this ban, you've taken away the discretion among doctors to act in the best interests of their patients. At this stage of the outbreak, how can you justify breaking the duty a doctor has with their patient all the way from Canberra, remotely?

agency: Department of Health, Disability and Ageing
text: I'll perhaps ask Professor Kidd to reflect on some of the response. You do reflect there on the duty of the doctors. There are a number of well-recognised duties that doctors hold towards their patient. They include such things as respecting the autonomy of the patient in their decision-making and respecting the confidentiality of the patient in their decision-making. But two other significant pillars of the doctor's duty are what we describe as beneficence and nonmaleficence. Nonmaleficence is to, first, do no harm. The decisions that were taken around restricting use of those medicines during COVID were related to ensuring that harm is not done—in that, patients were being convinced to take medicines that had no supportive evidence that they were effective for COVID. Also, it meant that those medicines were not available for other patients for whom they were needed for the actual approved indications. But the fourth duty that I described, that of beneficence, is that we should always be doing good for our patients, and it is difficult to reconcile the duty you describe with recommending treatments that have no supportive evidence indicating that they are useful for the indication which you're describing.
witness_organisation: Department of Health, Disability and Ageing
witness_position: Deputy Secretary, Health Products Regulation Group

agency: Department of Health, Disability and Ageing
text: Professor Lawler, you're not aware of the many, many papers? For example, Dr Pierre Kory in the states has listed, I think, over 100 papers that show ivermectin is effective.

agency: Department of Health, Disability and Ageing
text: Senator Roberts, we are going to have to wrap up—

agency: Department of Health, Disability and Ageing
text: Andhra Pradesh stopped COVID in its tracks by ivermectin.

agency: Department of Health, Disability and Ageing
text: because we are running out of time for this evening—

agency: Department of Health, Disability and Ageing
text: You're not aware of that?

agency: Department of Health, Disability and Ageing
text: and there are other senators who want the call.

agency: Department of Health, Disability and Ageing
text: I'm aware that—sorry, Chair.
witness_organisation: Department of Health, Disability and Ageing
witness_position: Deputy Secretary, Health Products Regulation Group

agency: Department of Health, Disability and Ageing
text: We're going to need to wrap this up here. Perhaps, if there's further information that can be provided to Senator Roberts, it can be done so on notice. Senator Ruston.

agency: Department of Health, Disability and Ageing
text:
Professor Lawler, I note that on 28 September there was a guidance issued by the TGA which was 'Determining when news is subject to the therapeutic goods advertising rules'. It says:

Under the Act, any statement, pictorial representation or design that is intended (whether directly or indirectly) to promote the use or supply of therapeutic goods is likely to be considered advertising.

… … … In a news and media context, content can be considered advertising where, assessed objectively and as a whole, it appears to be designed or calculated to draw public attention to and to promote the supply or use of the identified goods. This may be the case even where content is created for editorial, educational or public-interest purposes if it goes beyond informing the public and is presented in a way that promotes the use or supply of a therapeutic good.

The purpose of the guidance was to help journalists and news organisations distinguish between news reporting and advertising of therapeutic goods. Was this guidance developed in response to any particular pharmaceutical announcement?

agency: Department of Health, Disability and Ageing
text: The guidance wasn't in response to any specific announcement.
witness_organisation: Department of Health, Disability and Ageing
witness_position: First Assistant Secretary, Regulatory Practice and Support Division

agency: Department of Health, Disability and Ageing
text: So it was not intended to target news reports about the availability of drugs on the private market, particularly those that are not listed on the PBS?

agency: Department of Health, Disability and Ageing
text: No, Senator. There are a couple of specific questions there, I think, that are slightly different. There was not a specific therapeutic good that prompted it, but the driver for it was very much that there had been increasing frequency of advertising of therapeutic goods—those that are both on and off the therapeutic goods register. We see this particularly in the case of online advertising but also in mainstream media. We see it confluent with the increase in access to online telehealth and vertically integrated models. Our function at the TGA, particularly in our safeguarding of therapeutic goods advertising, is not related to whether medicines are on the PBS or not. They are related to the nature and the extent of the risk that they present to the public if they are advertised directly or indirectly.
witness_organisation: Department of Health, Disability and Ageing
witness_position: Deputy Secretary, Health Products Regulation Group

agency: Department of Health, Disability and Ageing
text: Your direction seems to be very clearly speaking to media as opposed to advertising. It talks about news stories, editorial content, journalists and news organisations. This is not talking traditionally in relation to advertising people; this is talking about people who provide news. I'm keen to understand the logic behind why it's written like this, because immediately, on the surface, this just looked like censorship to me. If a news outlet determines that a story about a particular pharmaceutical product is newsworthy enough for them to write a story, how does the TGA then go about deciding if that breaches some sort of advertising rules? What's the legal advice that sits behind your belief that what you've put here is appropriate under the three acts that you are talking about here? This is not talking about advertising; this is talking about media reports. I'm interested in understanding: how is it that you as the TGA, or your acts, determine what is newsworthy and what's not newsworthy?

agency: Department of Health, Disability and Ageing
text:
I'll ask Mr Bedford to add to my response, but I would just make a couple of observations. Firstly, part of the driver is that the distinction between media and news reporting and advertising is potentially not as hardline as we might like. In informal conversations with media outlets, particularly when we're talking about some of the medicines or other therapeutic goods that we're talking about, there actually were on occasion informal requests for guidance around whether this actually constitutes advertising under the act. This was not just to provide a compliance tool; it was also to provide guidance and support, and education and information, for media outlets.

The second thing I would say is that this is not the only element of our approach to addressing risks to the public presented by advertising. This is just one of a number of things. We frequently engage in public education exercises around what advertising means beyond that. There are a number of instances in which we've actually taken action on the advertising of therapeutic goods, and that can range anywhere from educational warning letters up to potentially civil and criminal penalties. In terms of, perhaps, what went into developing it and the legal backing, I'll ask Mr Bedford to respond.
witness_organisation: Department of Health, Disability and Ageing
witness_position: Deputy Secretary, Health Products Regulation Group

agency: Department of Health, Disability and Ageing
text: I think the other bit of context is last financial year we had about 300 inquiries asking about advertising and promotion of therapeutic goods, so there was a significant amount of interest in making sure our guidance was improved. We always try—
witness_organisation: Department of Health, Disability and Ageing
witness_position: First Assistant Secretary, Regulatory Practice and Support Division

agency: Department of Health, Disability and Ageing
text: Inquiries from whom?

agency: Department of Health, Disability and Ageing
text: From all different outlets and different people. I'd need to take it on notice if you wanted a list of the 300 different—
witness_organisation: Department of Health, Disability and Ageing
witness_position: First Assistant Secretary, Regulatory Practice and Support Division

agency: Department of Health, Disability and Ageing
text: No. I'm just interested in the types of people you're saying you got inquiries from. Were there inquiries from news outlets? Were there inquiries from consumers? Were there inquiries from drug companies? Were there inquiries from colleagues? Who was it from?

agency: Department of Health, Disability and Ageing
text: From news outlets, from pharmaceutical companies, sometimes from pharmacies—a whole range of different people that may be selling, promoting or reporting on different therapeutic goods.
witness_organisation: Department of Health, Disability and Ageing
witness_position: First Assistant Secretary, Regulatory Practice and Support Division

agency: Department of Health, Disability and Ageing
text: Another example is the number of healthcare professionals who are interested and engaged in education around what the best treatment options might be in heart disease or skin disease or a number of other things and want to be really clear around whether talking about a specific product or a specific medicine actually constitutes advertising. I know that it may seem easy for me to say this, but we're absolutely not in the business of censorship of free speech. But we need to recognise that there is a significant power imbalance, particularly when people hear information that isn't appropriately contextualised in a clinical sense or when people hear information such as testimonials or advertising from health professionals. It isn't always easy for members of the public to be able to make a judgement about whether something is a balanced claim, so this is about providing guidance. You'll see there that we don't say that this does or it doesn't; it says that this 'may' constitute advertising. That's because we believe and we think that we are most appropriately approaching this by taking each case on its merits.
witness_organisation: Department of Health, Disability and Ageing
witness_position: Deputy Secretary, Health Products Regulation Group

agency: Department of Health, Disability and Ageing
text: From what I've just read out, this guidance appears to be specifically about news reports. I don't know that I've ever heard of a situation where news media would ever ask if their stories were advertising, because I don't believe any of them ever thought they would be. And neither should they be. Media outlets also have very strong guidelines under which they have to operate within for their own jurisdictions—guidelines around the ethics of what they're allowed to do. This seemed more like an issue of the TGA's interpretation, but this was about media outlets and media reporting; it wasn't about the TGA's interpretation. I accept what you've said about what you do, but it seems to be somewhat in conflict with what is actually written in this determination.

agency: Department of Health, Disability and Ageing
text: What I'd say in response is that I take your comment that you've not seen statements in the media that would be easily confused with advertising—
witness_organisation: Department of Health, Disability and Ageing
witness_position: Deputy Secretary, Health Products Regulation Group

agency: Department of Health, Disability and Ageing
text: No, that isn't what I said.

agency: Department of Health, Disability and Ageing
text: I'm sorry, that's what I took from it—
witness_organisation: Department of Health, Disability and Ageing
witness_position: Deputy Secretary, Health Products Regulation Group

agency: Department of Health, Disability and Ageing
text: No. I was just saying that I don't believe that news media would believe that they are advertising when they provide news stories. I can't imagine a news media outlet picking up the phone and saying, 'I'm going to write a story about a particular drug'—I won't say it just in case I'm in breach by saying the name of a drug. They aren't going to ring you up and ask you, 'Is this advertising?' News outlets write stories because they believe they are newsworthy.

agency: Department of Health, Disability and Ageing
text: There is even a case currently before the courts that involves a news outlet that published a story that led to a class of medications. The thing to understand is that—
witness_organisation: Department of Health, Disability and Ageing
witness_position: First Assistant Secretary, Regulatory Practice and Support Division

agency: Department of Health, Disability and Ageing
text: Sorry, can you explain to me what the process was in that case? You're saying that there's currently a news story that a media outlet—

agency: Department of Health, Disability and Ageing
text: There is currently a case before the courts, which I can't go into further detail about because of—
witness_organisation: Department of Health, Disability and Ageing
witness_position: First Assistant Secretary, Regulatory Practice and Support Division

agency: Department of Health, Disability and Ageing
text: How did it come to be before the court? Was it something that—

agency: Department of Health, Disability and Ageing
text: The TGA is taking action.
witness_organisation: Department of Health, Disability and Ageing
witness_position: First Assistant Secretary, Regulatory Practice and Support Division

agency: Department of Health, Disability and Ageing
text: You've taken action.

agency: Department of Health, Disability and Ageing
text: Yes.
witness_organisation: Department of Health, Disability and Ageing
witness_position: First Assistant Secretary, Regulatory Practice and Support Division

agency: Department of Health, Disability and Ageing
text: Is that a recent case?

agency: Department of Health, Disability and Ageing
text: I think it's safe to say that it predated the release of this guidance.
witness_organisation: Department of Health, Disability and Ageing
witness_position: Deputy Secretary, Health Products Regulation Group

agency: Department of Health, Disability and Ageing
text: This one did.
witness_organisation: Department of Health, Disability and Ageing
witness_position: First Assistant Secretary, Regulatory Practice and Support Division

agency: Department of Health, Disability and Ageing
text: Did it predate it by a long way, or just a reasonably short period of time?

agency: Department of Health, Disability and Ageing
text: We have to rotate the call now.

agency: Department of Health, Disability and Ageing
text: I'll need to take the date on notice, unless Ms Sellars has the information in front of her. But I think that the important thing to understand is that any online content that directly or indirectly promotes the use or supply of a therapeutic good may be considered advertising. That goes to articles in newspapers too; social media and other things are much more prolific at the moment.
witness_organisation: Department of Health, Disability and Ageing
witness_position: First Assistant Secretary, Regulatory Practice and Support Division

agency: Department of Health, Disability and Ageing
text:
May I add just a couple of things? As I mentioned, this is just one element. We also have guidelines on advertising on social media and guidance for advertising by health professionals. So this is not a targeted issue for media. The other thing I would say is that there are significant instances where, firstly, we are contacted just to clarify whether this might be skirting advertising.

The other thing, though, is that if we have not been contacted and we do see coverage where media outlets have been advertising—and, hopefully, I'm not misinterpreting you again; these are instances where media don't ring us up because they're on a good story and they're going to be advertising—that's actually—
witness_organisation: Department of Health, Disability and Ageing
witness_position: Deputy Secretary, Health Products Regulation Group

agency: Department of Health, Disability and Ageing
text: You keep using the word 'advertising'. Being on a good story and telling a good story because the yarn they believe is newsworthy and it happens to relate to a particular medicine—you're calling this 'advertising'. The media outlet just say it's a newsworthy yarn that they want to tell the story about. I'm keen to understand how your act—maybe this is something to take on notice. I am concerned about what this is, and I'm happy to take it offline with you because I think this is real overreach on your part in relation to reaching into the jurisdiction of the media to write a yarn about something that they think is newsworthy and in the public interest, and I'm not quite sure how that all works. There is a very significant difference between advertising a product and a story. You seem to be confusing the two because you're talking about a news story that's advertising.

agency: Department of Health, Disability and Ageing
text: Given it seems like we're going around in circles here—

agency: Department of Health, Disability and Ageing
text: That's your interpretation.

agency: Department of Health, Disability and Ageing
text: perhaps the officials can take on notice some further detail to your answer, and then we can, whether it's a private briefing for the committee or some further discussions about this topic tomorrow—

agency: Department of Health, Disability and Ageing
text: Are you back tomorrow or not?

agency: Department of Health, Disability and Ageing
text: Absolutely.
witness_organisation: Department of Health, Disability and Ageing
witness_position: Deputy Secretary, Health Products Regulation Group

agency: Department of Health, Disability and Ageing
text: Lucky you!

agency: Department of Health, Disability and Ageing
text: I will pass the call to Senator Bleyer.

agency: Department of Health, Disability and Ageing
text: My questions continue to be on medical device regulations. We established that overseas warnings about device risks are passed on to users in Australia based on an applicability test. Are you able to succinctly define what is the inapplicability test?

agency: Department of Health, Disability and Ageing
text: There's no test per se that I can say is A plus B plus C equals 'do a market action'. We look at the nature of what the event may be. Sometimes there are small things where it's a software update and we work with the sponsor. Often, for these sorts of things, the sponsors come to the TGA directly; we don't need to go to them. Other times there might be bigger signals. They might be things that aren't necessarily a particular thing that's occurred but we're seeing a bit of a pattern. Overseas might be seeing a pattern and they're investigating it, so they might do a particular action. Other times we see patterns first, and we will investigate and undertake an action. It's a bit difficult to say, 'Here's a simple formula for it,' because it is on a case-by-case basis. That's on purpose because it is a risk based framework. We fundamentally want the public to have access to devices. We want those to be safe and to perform as intended, but we also want to make sure that we intervene whenever something is a risk to the public.
witness_organisation: Department of Health, Disability and Ageing
witness_position: Assistant Secretary, Medical Devices and Product Quality Division

agency: Department of Health, Disability and Ageing
text: That's a big responsibility as opposed to simply just passing on the overseas warning.

agency: Department of Health, Disability and Ageing
text: That's right. Sometimes the overseas warnings aren't necessarily applicable. With the way we register products, there might be multiple products under an ARTG entry. If we simply pass on a warning, that product may not be in the Australian public—so we might inadvertently scare the public from accessing important therapeutic goods because they see something that is not applicable to them. As Ms Duffy noted before, other times we pass on messages anyway. For example, we were concerned about the risk of some hyperbaric chambers, and there was, unfortunately, a death that occurred overseas. We knew those products weren't being used in the same way in Australia. Nonetheless, we published information on our website just in case there were members of the public accessing these products, to make sure that there were appropriate safeguards and that they had the information at hand.
witness_organisation: Department of Health, Disability and Ageing
witness_position: Assistant Secretary, Medical Devices and Product Quality Division

agency: Department of Health, Disability and Ageing
text: I understand, thank you. I'm sorry to hear that the TGA has had issues with staffing. I understand it had around half the staff it needed to monitor adverse event alerts in 2024, and that was before there was mandatory reporting. Mandatory reporting took effect in March this year and was expected to create a tenfold increase in reporting. Has there been an increase in reporting? Has it been tenfold? I hope you can tell me that you now have the staff to attend to that increase.

agency: Department of Health, Disability and Ageing
text: The mandatory reporting that you referred to is mandatory reporting via healthcare facilities in Australia, the 600-odd hospitals that started reporting certain incidents to the TGA. We can say that, over time, the number of staff in the medical devices postmarket area has increased. In fact, we now have a surveillance branch, but that was in place before the mandatory reporting started. In terms of the mandatory reporting and the numbers that are coming in, Dr Noja might have those numbers in terms of how many we've received from hospitals since the scheme started earlier this year.
witness_organisation: Department of Health, Disability and Ageing
witness_position: First Assistant Secretary, Medical Devices and Product Quality Division

agency: Department of Health, Disability and Ageing
text: We have had a large number of reports. On average we're having around 400 reports coming in a month through the mandatory reporting scheme. We have also had an increase in more general adverse event reports. What's really important about the increase in reports is the more reports we have, the more we are able to be really selective in the things that we investigate and the signals that we assess. It lets us shift from having to really search for signals to letting the signals come out in their earnest. Whilst we have had a significant increase in reports, our investigations haven't had to increase substantially, because what the increased reporting has shown us is that the sponsors who are fundamentally responsible for undertaking investigations are doing so, and we're able to be much more targeted in our work.
witness_organisation: Department of Health, Disability and Ageing
witness_position: Assistant Secretary, Medical Devices and Product Quality Division

agency: Department of Health, Disability and Ageing
text: Did you get additional funding to meet the demands?

agency: Department of Health, Disability and Ageing
text: We haven't had additional funding in respect to the mandatory reporting scheme. It is in its early days, but we are looking at our systems more broadly to ensure that they remain fit for purpose.
witness_organisation: Department of Health, Disability and Ageing
witness_position: Assistant Secretary, Medical Devices and Product Quality Division

agency: Department of Health, Disability and Ageing
text: Did you ask for more money and weren't given it?

agency: Department of Health, Disability and Ageing
text: The funding that we receive in the TGA to do medical device activities is cost-recovery funding. We either have fees for applicants or an annual charge for those suppliers, sponsors who have products that they continue to supply in Australia. The amount of funding that we allocate to our various activities is looked at on an annual basis, and we determine on an annual basis how much funding we divide between premarket work and postmarket work, noting the volumes and the work that might be expected to happen in the next year and then balance between the two areas of work with the funding that's available. Over time, as I mentioned before, the funding allocated to postmarket and postmarket monitoring has increased and shifted the balance, because that is where we've had to focus our efforts. It's because of that analysis we do.
witness_organisation: Department of Health, Disability and Ageing
witness_position: First Assistant Secretary, Medical Devices and Product Quality Division

agency: Department of Health, Disability and Ageing
text: My next question is about pelvic mesh. It's been associated with severe and life-changing complications and caused real damage. As I understand it, it got into the Australian market through the substantial equivalence pathway. That meant it avoided clinical trials, but the pathway still exists. Is that appropriate?

agency: Department of Health, Disability and Ageing
text: The pathway still exists, and it's still appropriate. I might ask Dr Cuss to explain the fact that our response to mesh has meant that the mesh products themselves are at a higher classification now and what that actually means.
witness_organisation: Department of Health, Disability and Ageing
witness_position: First Assistant Secretary, Medical Devices and Product Quality Division

agency: Department of Health, Disability and Ageing
text: It's a really relevant point because substantial equivalence is an appropriate form of assessment for products. In the case of pelvic mesh, back in 2016-17, when the Senate inquiry began, it was clear that some of the mesh products that had been approved and included in the ARTG were approved on the basis of more generalised indications—for example, support of soft tissues. As a result of that inquiry and the review that the TGA undertook at that time, we proceeded to implement quite a number of regulatory activities as a result. Part of that activity was to actually remove some of those meshes from use, from supply, but, as Ms Duffy said, one of the other activities that we undertook was to ensure that we then reviewed mesh in general a surgical meshes in general and we up-classified those products to a higher classification rate. What that means with respect to substantial equivalence is that those class 3, highest level medical devices, undergo quite a substantial and significantly robust assessment that looks at not just substantial equivalence but other information. Information in terms of evidence for a product can include comparisons to other devices, as you suggest, but also include evidence for the device itself, if there is evidence—direct clinical trials, clinical investigations—and it also includes other forms of evidence, such as registry information, which is very valuable. For example, if there's a registry in another country that's got quite a lot of evidence for that particular product, we can utilise that as well in our assessment.
witness_organisation: Department of Health, Disability and Ageing
witness_position: Medical Officer, Medical Devices and Product Quality Division

agency: Department of Health, Disability and Ageing
text: Thank you everyone for being here today, and we look forward to seeing you again tomorrow morning when we will continue this outcome.
